Point-by-point response to the reviewer’s comments
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
This paper is a well written and timely evaluation of the impacts of climate change on future
GoM ecosystem and fishery productivity. It is unique in the aspect that it connects climate
impacts on land (drought) to those in marine systems via changes in freshwater nutrient inputs to
GoM. This is an often postulated interaction (i.e., climate impacts on land and water will impact
marine systems) but there is a paucity of published papers that demonstrate or evaluate the
phenomenon. The authors use a combination of a nutrient-forced mass-balance ecosystem model
(EwE) and mean future climate projections of a drought index (PDSI) from an ensemble of 20
General Circulation Models (GCMs) representing a subset of CMIP5 ensemble members under
the high baseline Representative Carbon Pathway (RCP 8.5). The authors derived a linear
relationship between historical nutrients and historical PDSI values and used the nutrient
relationship to drive bottom up productivity changes in the EwE model.
The authors then force the EwE model with profiles across ranges in nutrient changes (0 -2 fold
2014-2016 average nutrient levels) and ranges in fishing pressure (0-5 x average F from 2014-
2016). This represents an innovative application of an approach that has been applied
successfully to evaluate potential climate change impacts in other systems, albeit with different
climate couplings (e.g., where temperature or zooplankton drive productivity of EwE models;
sensu https://doi.org/10.1111/gcb.13471 ). In general this is the type of analysis that can be vital
for risk assessments of climate change impacts on marine fisheries as well as cumulative impacts
of changes on land on marine ecosystems. In general, I strongly support this type of approach,
and applaud the authors for using an ecosystem model (which captures indirect and cascading
impacts) to evaluate climate change impacts on marine species. This can be a more robust
approach than a direct climate-linked single species
modeling effort.
However, there are a number of fundamental issues with the paper that I believe preclude it from
being published until it is revised. I hope the authors are able to correct and address these issues
so it can be used to advance understanding of climate change risk to marine ecosystems and
fisheries.
We thank the reviewer for the positive comments. In the revised manuscript, we have
thoroughly addressed the concerns raised by incorporating additional analyses, integrating
new data, and expanding the relevant sections as needed. We have also included the
citation of Woodworth-Jefcoats et al. (2017) in the text to enhance context and support our
findings.
The largest concern I have is that the paper is predicated on a linkage between droughts and
historical declines in GoM catches that the authors do not demonstrate and which is not
supported by the cited peer-reviewed papers (nor by the large number of non-peer reviewed
technical reports that are cited). The authors postulate that a long (~3 year) drought in the mid- to
late 1980’s induced a decline in biomass and catch that is reflected in the timeseries for both.
These are plotted in Figure 1 (a) (e) and (f). However, one quickly notes that there are similar
large drops in the PDSI index in ~2000 and ~2012 but no similar subsequent drop in catch or
biomass timeseries as was seen in the late 1980’s. In the discussion section (lines 160-172) the
authors try to address this and explain it as a difference in drought length (3 yrs for the earlier
drought versus ~1 year for the others) and timing. This section is very speculative, without any
citations save for one at the end of the paragraph stating that the severity of the drought can be
related to the contrast between preceding wet years. In fact the largest concern I had in reading
this section was that there was no mention of possible changes in fishery management or markets
that could also explain the decline in catch.
We appreciate the reviewer's insightful comments regarding the linkage between droughts
and historical declines in Gulf of Mexico (GoM) catches. As noted in our manuscript, we
hypothesize that significant ecosystem impacts, reflected in declines in biomass and catches,
would primarily occur following prolonged severe droughts lasting three years or more.
This hypothesis is based on the understanding that short-lived species, such as Gulf
menhaden, can typically rebound through density-dependent compensatory processes after
brief periods of low productivity. However, extended periods of low productivity can
severely affect multiple year-classes, leading to long-term detrimental impacts on these
populations. We further clarify that the apparent effects of the 1980s drought can be partly
attributed to (1) elevated biomass and catches during the mid-1980s, following
exceptionally wet conditions in early 1982-1983, and (2) the high fishing effort prevalent
throughout the 1980s. (3) our extended time series (Supplementary section S2)
demonstrates that episodic fluctuations in menhaden populations correlate with highly dry
conditions (e.g., 2006, 2012) and wet periods (e.g., 2010).
To further address the reviewer’s concerns, we acknowledge that variations in fishery
management practices and market dynamics over time might also contribute to
fluctuations in catch. In the revised manuscript, we have included additional discussion on
these factors to provide a more comprehensive context for the observed changes in catch
and biomass.
Additionally, in response to the reviewer’s suggestion regarding the speculative nature of
the discussion, we have incorporated a new Supplementary section S6, which includes a
sensitivity analysis that evaluates the effects of prolonged versus shorter drought periods
(1- and 3- years duration). This analysis quantifies the potential impacts of different
drought durations and strengthens the robustness of our findings.
Additionally, following the sharp drop in in both catches and biomass in the late 1980’s catches
remain low while biomass increases, pointing towards a non-biomass driver of low catches (e.g.,
shift in management towards lower harvest mortality rates).
We appreciate the reviewer’s observations regarding the dynamics of catches and biomass
in the late 1980s. Indeed, from 1992 onwards, after the drought of the late 1980s, we
observed a gradual decline in catches, averaging approximately 3 t/km² over 24 years. This
trend aligns with the expected relationship described by the equation (C = F×B), where
fishing mortality (F) was reduced due to regulatory measures, consequently leading to
declining annual catches. This regulatory action facilitated an increase in the remaining
biomass within the marine ecosystem, fostering a more sustainable fish population.
To clarify this we added supplementary section S3, which illustrates the contrasting
relationship between menhaden catches and fishing effort in the 1980s (a non-intuitive,
drought-dominated relationship) and the shift towards a more intuitive relationship from
the 1990s onward.
Finally there are multiple disparate patterns in the magnitude and sometimes the direction of
biomass change and catch (this can be seen in Fig 1 (h) and (i); e.g., crab have the second largest
decline in biomass but increases in catch, similarly, younger menhaden had the larger declines in
biomass than older conspecifics but declines in older menhaden catches were larger than younger
ones). This is of course a not unexpected and well cited issue in fisheries, especially as biomass
declines where fishers can increase effort to offset declining biomass, or where catch declines
but is stabilized over time and biomass increases due to implementation of policies that reduce
harvest rates to sustainable levels. I believe the authors are aware of this issue (see plots of
relative effort) and offer what is maybe the most parsimonious explanation in the “model
limitation” section of the Methods (lines 506 -509):
506 “...For example, fluctuations in Gulf menhaden catches may be related to economic
processes, which occurred during the mid and late 1980s, when the Gulf menhaden fishery
underwent corporate consolidation resulting in declines in the number of fishing vessels and
processing plants. This may have contributed to the decline in catches 45. For species such as
Goliath grouper, declines in biomass and catch are likely a result of long periods of overfishing
or management regulations designed to reduce harvest (e.g., harvest moratorium).”
Similarly, the ESR (reference #1) states “The Gulf of Mexico Fisheries Management Council
implemented a number of Fishery Management Plans in the 1980s, and major Amendments
restricting fishing effort were passed in the 1990s.“ (p22).
We appreciate the reviewer’s valuable comment regarding the complex patterns observed
in biomass changes and catch dynamics. In addition, we indeed recognize that the
fluctuations in biomass and catch, such as the decline in crab biomass coinciding with an
increase in catch, are well-documented phenomena in fisheries science. To address these
complexities, we have enriched the "model limitation" section with further explanations
about the economic and regulatory factors at play, including the historical context of the
Gulf menhaden fishery and relevant management measures implemented over the years.
Additionally, we have included a non-fisheries-related index of juvenile Gulf menhaden
abundance in Louisiana estuaries. This data reveals a decline in the juvenile Gulf
menhaden population during the late 1980s that is unrelated to fisheries management
measures, further highlighting the influence of external environmental factors.
Of course these management measures could have been implemented to address the decline that
was driven initially by drought. The way to address how much climate drove the decline is to run
a hindcast or counterfactual simulation, although these are challenging with ecosystem models
because of model drift. So another approach would be to use a sensitivity simulation to evaluate
the hypothesis of prolonged drought versus short 1 year drought in driving declines. E.g., fixing
the F rate at a few different levels (e.g., those observed in the 1985-1990 period vs those
observed in 2013), simulate a) 3 year drought (sensu the 1985-1988) and b) a five year period
with a 1 year drought. Something like this should be conducted to demonstrate and support the
postulation that underlies the projection simulations. In the absence of the sensitivity simulation
above, there is not sufficient evidence provided presently to rule out changes in harvest pressure,
fisheries operations, management or markets in driving declines in catch in the late 1980’s
relative to early 1980’s. Given that the paper is predicated on the postulated relationship between
drought, nutrients, and declines in catches, establishing and supporting this is extremely
important. Additionally, I strongly suggest providing a historical time-series of harvest mortality
by age for menhaden (e.g., as a supplemental figure). It appears to my eye that the F rate for 1
year old fish is much higher during the 1985-1990 period than 2000 - 2016. Having the
timeseries would help facilitate comparisons in relative fishing pressure over time.
We thank the reviewer for the valuable insights. In response to the comments, we have
included a sensitivity analysis in supplementary section S6 that evaluates the effects of
different drought durations, specifically simulating both 1-year and 3-year droughts under
variable F rates, in addition to the previously discussed 5-year drought scenario. This
analysis illustrates a clear correlation between the duration of drought and the cumulative
decline in biomass.
Additionally, we have incorporated the requested historical time series of harvest mortality
by age for Gulf menhaden, which can be found in Figure S2c. As noted by the reviewer,
this time series confirms that fishing mortality was indeed higher during the late 1980s
compared to the subsequent period from 2000 to 2016. This rise in fishing mortality during
the late 1980s can be attributed to higher fishing efforts and catches, while the later period
experienced lower fishing effort, which ultimately supported a gradual recovery of the
menhaden population.
Importantly, our findings suggest that changes in harvest pressure and fisheries operations
cannot fully account for the observed trends. As detailed in supplementary section S2,
menhaden fishing effort was actually declining during the 1980s, coinciding with a decline
in biomass, rather than the expected increase that would typically drive such reductions.
The second issue with the paper is that it is very difficult to discern precisely what methods were
used in the simulations. This needs to be clarified in the Methods simulation section. I have
detailed a number of line by line suggestions below to help clarify. There were two separate
simulations conducted. For the first, I believe the correct methods were used for the status quo
versus future time series projections, but can’t confirm this based on the current methods section.
For the first simulation, the authors ran the EwE model for a 5 year simulation period across
Nutrient and F profiles based on average 2014-2016 values for each (Navg2014-2016 and
Favg2014-2016). Within the intervals for each (Nutrients = (0,2) X Navg2014-2016 and F =
(0,5) x Favg2014-2016) is the value of 1.0, i.e., a simulation where N = N_avg and F = F_avg.
For the second the authors used linear regression to extrapolate the nutrient levels from the PDSI
projections for the first and second halves of the century. For both analyses it is not clear what
the baseline status quo scenario includes. Can the authors confirm that in lines 471-475,
comparisons of climate change simulations are relative to the terminal year of a 5 year control
simulation where N =Navg2014-2016 and F = Favg2014-2016 rather than comparisons directly
to 2016 values? This is important because ecosystem models can propagate error when adjusting
to new forcings and including a control run helps establish that differences are due to forcings
rather than model behavior. If this was done the authors need to clarify the start and end dates of
each simulation and in figure and the results consistently use a term like “persistence simulation”
or “control” rather than “2016” which is confusing. A table or figure of the simulation
methodology would greatly help clarify the two simulations.
We sincerely thank the reviewer for the valuable feedback regarding the clarity of our
methods in the simulations. In response, we have made several revisions to enhance the
clarity of our methodology. We have changed the text to include “Ecosim simulations” and
“Quantifying changes biomass and catches” sections and added detailed explanations to
enhance clarity. In the “Quantifying changes biomass and catches” section, we specifically
divided the methodologies into distinct sections: "Historical Perspective" and "Future
Perspective," clearly outlining the methods used in both analyses.
In the "Historical Perspective," we have elaborated on how we examined the differences
between pre-drought conditions (1982-1986) and drought-affected conditions (1988-1992),
utilizing historical time series data and EwE time-dynamic Ecosim Model simulations. We
included a detailed description of the equation used to analyze biomass and catches, as well
as explaining how the fishing mortality and nutrient input forcing for Gulf menhaden were
derived and implemented.
In the "Future Perspective," we specified our approach to quantifying changes in biomass
and catches in response to projected drought conditions, accounting for varying levels of
Gulf menhaden fishing mortality in a trade-off analysis. We highlighted the
implementation of a 5-year simulated drought and the use of linear regression to project
nutrient inputs based on PDSI data. We also clarified how terminal biomass was expressed
relative to the status quo and how relative changes in biomass and catch were calculated.
Furthermore, we used our sensitivity analysis simulations, which examine trade-offs
between nutrient input and Gulf menhaden fishing mortality, detailing how we modeled
nutrient loading and fishing mortality using various multipliers.
Regarding the baseline status quo scenario. To clarify, we confirm that the comparisons of
climate change simulations presented in lines 471-475 are indeed relative to the terminal
year of a 5-year control simulation, in which nutrient inputs N =geom_mean(N ) and
2014-2016
F = geom_mean(F ), rather than being directly compared to 2016 values.
2014-2016
In response to the reviewer’s suggestions, we have provided additional clarification
regarding the start and end dates of each simulation in the revised manuscript. We have
also standardized terminology, using the term “status quo scenario” consistently
throughout the text to avoid any confusion with the term “2016.”. Furthermore, we have
added a table (supplementary Table S6) that outlines all simulations along with detailed
explanations of each simulation.
For the second simulation, it is not clear from the Methods which years are included in this
extrapolation; values are reported in the Results section and Figure 2.b but again it is difficult to
understand which years are included in the values as they are reported as “anticipated by 2050
and during 2051-2100). It appears they are averages of 2016-2050 and 2051-2100. Are they the
mean of the 20 member ensemble for each year or the mean of all values from all simulations
within those time frames? There is considerable range in the PDSI of the 20 member ensemble
by end of the century and the upper range of the index ensemble mean includes values (PDSI>0)
seen in non-drought years. As such I strongly suggest that the authors run the simulation for
random draws from the mean and standard deviation of the ensemble for each time-period (e.g.,
100 draws) in order to provide error bars for the figures in Fig. 2c; confidence intervals around
projected declines may be large.
We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comments regarding the second simulation. The
drought conditions for the specified years were computed based on the minimal moving
average of the 5th percentile PDSI value over a 5-year period, utilizing the variation from
the 20-member CMIP ensemble. This approach allows us to focus on the driest consistent
spells, which are of particular interest in our study. The correspondence between the driest
observed PDSI (indicated by magenta markers in Fig. 2a) and the modeled PDSI
(represented by the yellow shaded area) in Fig. 2a further justifies our emphasis on the 5th
percentile of the modeled PDSI.
While we acknowledge that wet periods corresponding to positive PDSI values will occur
within the projected time frames (through the end of the century), our focus on the impacts
of droughts necessitates prioritizing drought periods over wet ones. It is important to note
that the PDSI index is a "long-memory" index that accounts for soil moisture; thus, the
effects of very wet periods can diminish quickly following extreme hot and dry conditions.
We have accepted the reviewer’s suggestion to utilize random draws (N=43 for each
scenario) from the mean and standard deviation of the ensemble for each time period in
order to provide error bars for the figures in Fig. 2c. We used the 5th percentile of the
modeled PDSI as the basis for our analysis based on the explanation above.
A growing number of papers include comparisons of projections of high and low carbon
emission scenarios, e.g., RCP8.5 vs RCP2.6 or the more recent CMIP6 SSP126 vs SSP 585.
These types of comparisons are extremely useful in IPCC and other climate assessments because
they reveal the relative risk of different levels of greenhouse gas emissions. To repeat this
analysis for RCP2.6 would be a major undertaking and so I am not suggesting that has to be done
here, but including multiple carbon emission scenarios is something the authors might consider
in future work as it would help address an important need for relative climate risk information
for fisheries and marine ecosystems.
We appreciate the reviewer’s comments regarding the inclusion of comparisons between
high and low carbon emission scenarios. In light of this, we have added text in the
discussion section to address the potential for including various RCP scenarios in future
research, with a specific focus on the implications of greenhouse gas emission mitigation
and management for fisheries and marine ecosystems.
In summary, I find the paper topic to be compelling, the methodology is established but novelly
applied, and the figures and text are clear and well executed. I appreciate the inclusion of the
code and data. If the authors are able to address the aforementioned concerns (and following line
by line suggestions) I believe that this paper can be an important contribution to the field of
climate change and fisheries. While these suggestions are not trivial I also believe that they are
achievable revisions that will immensely strengthen the paper.
We sincerely thank the reviewer for the positive feedback and encouraging remarks about

Line 416 “good agreement” how so? Provide a metric of skill or correlation.
We appreciate the reviewer’s inquiry regarding the phrase “good agreement” and the
request for metrics of skill or correlation. By "good agreement," we refer primarily to the
visual inspection of the time series fits. Additionally, we observed notable consistency
between the model-predicted estimates of the fishing mortality rate corresponding to the
maximum sustainable yield (FMSY) and the FMSY estimates obtained from stock
assessments (Berenshtein et al., 2023).
In addition, in response to the reviewer’s concern, we calculated the Modeling Efficiency
(MEF), a statistical metric that assesses how effectively our model predicts observed data
compared to using the mean of the observed values. While Ecosim models do not typically
yield a single measure of overall skill, modeling efficacy is often evaluated relative to the
model itself through Relative Model Efficiency (RME) and the Akaike Information
Criterion (AIC), as noted by Olsen et al. (2016).
Our analysis indicates that 74% of the fitted time series yielded positive MEF values,
suggesting that the model’s predictions are more accurate than those based on the mean of
the observed data for roughly three-quarters of the assessed time series. We have added
this information to the Methods section and included a supplementary section
(supplementary Section S5) that explains the assessment of Ecosim model fits, accompanied
by a table of MEF values (supplementary Table S5).
Notably, as explained in (Berenshtein et al., 2021, 2023) the time series that did not fit well
primarily involved highly migratory species and the early life stages of various groups,
which pose challenges for the EwE framework. This finding highlights the predictive
capacity of our model, although we acknowledge that the application of MEF is not
standard practice in Ecopath with Ecosim (EwE) modeling, complicating direct
comparisons with other EwE models.

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
In the ms by Berenshtein et al., the authors present data that indicates a severe drought in the
southeast U.S., combined with fishing pressure on ecologically important menhaden in the Gulf
of Mexico, likely caused a decline in marine food webs and fisheries catch in the 1980s. Using
these results the authors modeled future fisheries in the GoM under simulated drought
conditions. First, I would like to thank the authors for expanding the knowledge on the
ecosystem dynamics of this region, and further exploring the role of freshwater/nutrient inputs in
ocean ecosystems. I believe this could add to the growing body of knowledge to an important
socio-ecological system. With that said, I believe there are too many confounding factors that
could contribute to the lack of nutrients being the main driver to population dynamics in the
region, and this would be important for informing a more robust predictive model, and thus
should be considered before publication.
We thank the reviewer for their thoughtful comments on our manuscript and for
recognizing the contribution of our work. We appreciate the insights regarding the
confounding factors that may influence nutrient dynamics and population dynamics in the
region. We address the reviewer’s concerns in detail in the following replies to ensure the
robustness of our findings.
For the “historic” analysis on trends, I was a bit underwhelmed by the focus on 1982-86, then
1986-1992. The authors use these two time series to compare trends in fisheries and
environmental factors with the sole focus on drought and freshwater inputs. Why not include the
entire time series in an analysis that includes nutrient load relationships with fisheries, but also
the other known factors that influence marine food webs, such as temperature, wind/hurricanes,
and the elephant in the room…hypoxia? I think if this ms is to be published then it will be
important to apply quantitative analytical approaches on a beautiful historic time series that
should be able to tease apart the influence of these various environmental factors from 1980-
2016. I think without this analysis then the model is not fully informed. For example, in the time
series in Fig. 1a, there appears to be two other significant drought events in the region 1997-2000
and 2011-2014 (eyeballing), but fish biomass (Fig. 1e) is stable or going up during those periods.
What can explain that?
We thank the reviewer for the insightful comment. In this revised version, we have
included several sections that successfully address the reviewer’s comments. First, we
explain in more detail why the effect of the 1980s drought is much more pronounced
compared to other drought events. First, the duration of the severe drought conditions
were for more than three years, inflicts a tremendous impact on short-lived fisheries such
as the Gulf menhaden, which life span is approximately four years. In these conditions the
weak year-classes three years in a row severely diminish the population, especially as other
“non-estuary-dependent” species may utilize the diminishing population niche (e.g.,
Cephalopods), taking advantage of menhaden’s reduced density. In contrast, in an event of
an extreme drought of a single year, the other menhaden’s year classes, that were less
affected by the drought, compensate and “enjoy” more resources due to the new-year
diminished population, hence maintaining the overall health of the population. Second,
fishing pressure on Gulf menhaden was much higher in the 1980s, leading to fewer
spawners and reduced food for predators. Third, during this time, the fishery industry
underwent changes that decreased the number of fishing vessels, further affecting catch
rates. Lastly, the wet years before the drought boosted fish populations, making the
drought's negative effects more noticeable. In accordance with the above explanation, we
have added supplementary section S5, which examines the predicted change in biomass
and catches under conditions of one year, three years, and five years (as presented in the
main text) of drought conditions. In addition, we have added Supplementary section S2,
which includes numerous additional time series related to Gulf menhaden, Hypoxia index,
and named Hurricanes, demonstrating the correspondence between drought-related
conditions with menhaden population dynamics, and the lack of such correspondence with
other environmental factors such as SST, hypoxic area, and hurricanes.
Other Comments:

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
Review Berenshtein et al - Will mega-droughts in the US drive the collapse of fisheries in the
Gulf of Mexico?
This paper looks at the relationship between drought conditions and fisheries production in the
Gulf of Mexico. These relationships are reproduced in an ecosystem model that is then used at
the implications of climate change driven droughts into the future.
The authors have obviously put a lot of effort into revising the paper based on previous feedback.
The paper is well written and there are no typos or minor changes like that required. However, I
feel there is some further clarification required in a few spots as described below.
We thank the reviewer for their positive assessment of our revisions and writing, and we
appreciate their careful review of the updated manuscript.
• Line 105 “decline of 16% in the relative fishing effort by the purse menhaden fleet”: Is there
any tech creep to consider?
We thank the reviewer for this valuable comment. There is no explicit evidence for
technological creep (i.e., gradual improvements in fishing efficiency due to advances in
vessel or gear technology) during the 1980s that could cause nominal effort to decrease
while actual effective effort remained stable or increased. Rather, studies (e.g., Vaughan et
al., 2007) attribute the observed decline in nominal purse-seine effort in that period to
explicit reductions in the number of vessels and processing plants, driven by corporate
acquisitions, company downsizing, and industrial consolidation. We have clarified this
point in the revised manuscript (lines 127-130) as follows: “Within this broader stability, the
menhaden purse-seine fleet did show a 16% reduction in relative effort (Fig. 1k), though this
has been attributed to decreases in fleet size and processing capacity, driven by corporate
acquisitions, downsizing, and industrial consolidation, rather than improvements in efficiency
or changes in fishing pressure”.
• Line 116: Because the methods are at the end, please explain what it is on first use as s not all
readers will know.
We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. The term in question is the Palmer Drought
Severity Index (PDSI). In the revised manuscript, we now spell out the full name and
provide a concise definition at its first mention in the Results section (lines 108--109) as
follows:” Palmer’s Drought Severity Index (PDSI; a standard measure of drought intensity)”.
• Line 135-138 “The effect of Gulf menhaden fishing mortality on the cumulative biomass and
catch dynamics is smaller compared to the effect of anticipated droughts (Fig. 2c), suggesting
that the ability of the ecosystem to compensate for menhaden harvest is compromised under
drought conditions.”: Have you tried to run it with the broken stick harvest control rule in closed
loop mode to see if that helps recovery time? What about effort drops as seen in the historical
period?
We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. While we have not simulated the
broken stick harvest control rule in closed-loop mode, we did explore a wide range of effort
reductions and increases when generating the contour plots in Figures 2d–f. These
simulations are not identical to replicating the precise historical effort trajectories, but they
do capture the consequences of varying fishing pressure on biomass and recovery dynamics
under different drought scenarios. Together, they provide partial insight into the
reviewer’s question regarding effort drops. Exploring fully dynamic harvest control rules
and explicitly testing historical effort patterns remain promising avenues for future
research, particularly for assessing adaptive management strategies that could mitigate
drought impacts. We now highlight this point in the Discussion (lines 224--228) as follows:
“Notably, while we did not simulate harvest control rules (e.g., broken-stick) in our projection,
our contour-plot analyses (Figs. 2d–f) spanned a wide range of fishing mortality levels under
drought. These results provide partial insight into effort reductions, though explicit tests of
dynamic harvest rules and historical effort trajectories remain an important direction for
future work.”.
• Line 146: Rationale for the specific x2 increase?
We thank the reviewer for requesting clarification. The two-fold increase corresponds to
the maximum observed value in the historical range of variation for this parameter,
ensuring that the scenario represents an extreme yet empirically grounded case. We have
clarified this rationale in the Results section (lines 177-181) as follows: ” For status quo
nutrient input and increased (x2) Gulf menhaden fishing mortality conditions, corresponding
to the maximum value observed historically (1980–2016 relative to 2016), there is a decrease
in the biomass of several groups: Gulf menhaden, their associated predators, species that are
bycatch in the menhaden purse seine fleet (e.g., sea trout), and other species that decline due
to indirect trophic interactions.”.
• Line 149-150 “In contrast, the biomass of the competitors of these groups (e.g., cephalopods),
increases (Fig. 3a).”: Are technical interactions accounted for?
We thank the reviewer for this question. Yes, technical interactions are accounted for in
our EwE model through the explicit linkage of each fleet to all functional groups it exploits
through harvest and discards, based on observed catch composition and gear selectivity.
We have clarified this point in the Results section (lines 190-192) as follows: “These
dynamics explicitly account for technical interactions, as fleets in the model are linked to
multiple functional groups through both targeted catch and bycatch based on observed
composition and selectivity.”.
• Line 213 “jellyfish, become more dominant”: Possible to comment on cascading implications?
We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. In the revised manuscript, we now briefly
elaborate on the potential cascading implications of increased jellyfish dominance.
Specifically, jellyfish blooms can reduce prey availability for planktivorous fish and
compete with larval stages of many fish species for zooplankton resources, potentially
impairing recruitment success and altering trophic energy flow. These cascading effects are
now mentioned in the discussion. We have clarified this point in the Discussion section
(lines 289-292) as follows: “Such jellyfish dominance could have cascading effects, as blooms
reduce prey availability for planktivorous fish and compete with the larval stages of many fish
species for zooplankton resources, potentially impairing recruitment success and altering
trophic energy flow.”.
• Line 231-233 “This is supported, for example, by the low cumulative biomass and catches
during 1988 (Fig. 1), which was characterized by the lowest nutrient input, and consequently
lowest hypoxic area during the considered period25 (supplementary section S2, Figs. S1-2).”:
This is an argument by absence rather than unpacking of attribution when both present, not as

We thank the reviewer for this observation and agree with the concern raised. In the
revised text, we have modified our response to emphasize that our interpretation is
supported by: (1) the generally negative relationship observed between biomass, nutrient
input, and catches versus hypoxic area across multiple years; and (2) the well-established
mechanistic understanding that reduced nutrient input can limit primary productivity,
thereby lowering biomass and catches, even when hypoxic area is minimal. We have
clarified this point in the Discussion section (lines 310-314) as follows: “This interpretation
is further supported by the generally negative relationship observed across years between
biomass, nutrient input, and catches versus hypoxic area, and by the well-established
mechanism through which reduced nutrient input lowers primary productivity and,
consequently, biomass and catches, for example, in years such as 1988, 2000, and 2012, when
hypoxic area was minimal (Fig. 1, supplementary section S3, Figs. S2–3).”.
• General comment on the end of the discussion: Would it be fair to characterise the results as an
example of the pattern of the forcing function on production being amplified up the model vs less
F effects? This pattern of differential sensitivity has been seen before in EwE comparative work
(e.g. Fulton and Smith 2004 Afr. J. Mar. Sci. 26: 219–243). If it is this might be a point for
flagging caution and uncertainty around the results of the work.
We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. We agree that our results may reflect,
at least in part, the EwE model’s tendency to show stronger ecosystem-wide responses to
external forcing functions (e.g., changes in primary productivity) compared to changes in
fishing mortality, as reported in previous comparative studies such as Fulton and Smith
(2004). In the revised Discussion, we now highlight this as a potential source of uncertainty
and caution when interpreting the relative magnitudes of drought versus fishing effects in
our simulations. At the same time, we do not interpret this pattern as a systematic bias of
EwE models. Rather, it reflects the fundamental difference in the scope of these drivers:
changes in primary productivity inherently cascade through many trophic levels and
functional groups, whereas changes in fishing mortality tend to be more targeted in scope.
This distinction is especially important in the Gulf of Mexico, where nutrient inputs from
the Mississippi River are massive and represent a primary driver of ecosystem
productivity. Thus, while EwE may emphasize the broad reach of bottom-up forcing
relative to fishing effects, the strong drought effect observed in our simulations is consistent
with empirical evidence for bottom-up control in the Gulf, lending confidence to the
qualitative direction of our findings. We have added a paragraph in the Discussion (lines
236-247) to reflect this point as follows: “Our results may also reflect a broader pattern noted
in EwE comparative studies (e.g., Fulton and Smith, 2004), where external forcing functions
such as changes in primary productivity tend to propagate more strongly through food webs
than changes in fishing mortality. This differential sensitivity should not be interpreted as a
systematic bias in the EwE framework. Instead, it reflects the fundamental difference that
productivity changes cascade across many trophic levels and functional groups, while fishing
mortality is more targeted in scope. In the GoM, where nutrient inputs from the Mississippi
River are massive and act as a primary driver of ecosystem productivity, such bottom-up
forcing is expected to have particularly broad consequences. While we acknowledge this
distinction as a source of uncertainty when comparing the relative magnitudes of drought and
fishing effects, the strong drought effects observed in our simulations remain consistent with
empirical evidence for bottom-up control in the region, lending confidence to the qualitative
direction of our findings.”.
• Line 411 “1982-1986 and 1988-1992”: What is the comparability of environmental conditions
and human use in general (so can isolate the drought effect)?
We thank the reviewer for this question. The two periods, 1982–1986 and 1988–1992,
were selected to bracket the 1988 drought, enabling a comparison of pre- and post-drought
conditions. Examination of environmental indicators (Fig. 1, Fig. S2, previously Fig. S1)
shows that, apart from the sharp drought-related drop in PDSI, river discharge, and
nutrient load in 1988, the two periods are broadly comparable: SST anomalies are similar
in magnitude and variability, and river and nutrient inputs partially recover in the later
period. Human-use indicators, such as relative fishing effort per fleet, are also comparable
between the periods, with no evidence for major technological or regulatory changes, and
interannual variability remains within historical ranges. The lower catches and biomass
observed in 1988–1992 coincide with the nutrient decline rather than changes in fishing
pressure. While we acknowledge the potential influence of other environmental and
anthropogenic factors, these similarities suggest that the observed differences primarily
reflect the drought effect. To address this point, we clarified in the Results section (lines
123-126) that environmental and human-use indicators were broadly comparable across
the two periods, supporting the interpretation that the observed differences are primarily
attributable to the drought as follows: “Importantly, aside from the sharp drought-related
reductions in PDSI, river discharge, and nutrient inputs in 1988, other environmental
indicators (e.g., SST anomalies) and overall fishing effort levels were broadly comparable
between the two periods (Fig. 1, Fig. S2), supporting the interpretation that the observed
declines primarily reflect the drought effect.”.
• Line 415 “computations of cumulative biomass”: This is aggregate biomass correct? It is likely
fine as it is but aggregate is probably the more commonly used term.
We thank the reviewer for this clarification. Yes, “cumulative biomass” in this context
refers to the aggregate biomass summed across all functional groups in the model. In the
revised text, we have added a note indicating that this term is equivalent to aggregate
biomass. A clarification note was added in the Results section (lines 119-121), as follows:
“Analysis of historical fisheries data indicates a loss of 41.742% in cumulative biomass (i.e.,
aggregate biomass summed across all functional groups) and 34.1% in cumulative catch
during the periods of 1988-1992 compared to 1982-1986”.
• Line 429 “Discards for other fisheries were not incorporated into catch time series.”:
Implications? Estimate of how big a biomass take this was? Some groups effected more than
others?
We thank the reviewer for raising this point. In general, discards from other fisheries were
not systematically incorporated into the Ecosim catch time series because consistent
historical data were not available across the full study period. For most functional groups,
catch time series were constructed from NOAA landings data, meaning that discards were
largely excluded. An exception is assessed species (e.g., red snapper, groupers, king
mackerel, sharks, tunas) for which SEDAR assessments report total removals (landings +
dead discards); in these cases, the Ecosim inputs generally included both components.
Thus, while discard mortality is partially represented for assessed species, it is likely
underrepresented for other groups, especially non-target bycatch species and those
primarily interacting with shrimp trawls and reef fisheries.
Available records indicate that discards in the Gulf of Mexico outside the menhaden
fishery represent a relatively small share of total removals at the ecosystem scale. While
including discard biomass would slightly increase total removals and could influence
biomass trends for some groups, we expect the ecosystem-level patterns and the relative
contrast between drought- and fishing-driven impacts to remain robust. We have added a
note in the Discussion (lines 315-322) to acknowledge this limitation, along with its
implications for certain functional groups that are more discard-prone, as follows:
“Another limitation relates to discards. While discard mortality was partially represented for
some assessed species where total removals (landings + dead discards) were available, it is
likely underrepresented for other commercial and especially recreational fisheries. Available
records suggest that discards constitute a relatively small proportion of total removals at the
ecosystem scale, but they can be substantial for certain groups, particularly small pelagics,
juvenile demersals, and non-target invertebrates. Incorporating more complete discard
information in future models could refine biomass estimates for these groups, though we do
not expect it to alter the overall contrast between drought- and fishing-driven effects reported
here.”.
• Line 464-465 “linear least squares regression to model the relationship between historical
nutrient input and the Palmer Drought Severity Index”: What about potential for changed
agricultural practices due to hypoxia concern? Implications of land use from ISIMIP
(https://www.isimip.org/) runs?
We thank the reviewer for this important point. Our regression assumes the historical
relationship between nutrient input and PDSI is primarily driven by hydrological
variability and does not account for long-term changes in agricultural practices. In the
Mississippi–Atchafalaya River Basin, conservation measures since the 1980s have reduced
nitrogen loads by 5–34% in high-intensity areas (García et al., 2016), though phosphorus
reductions have been weaker. These gains are often offset by hydroclimate variability, with
~72% of monthly nitrogen load variability since 1980 attributed to climate and extreme-
flow years delivering ≈30% higher loads (Lu et al., 2020). Thus, while agricultural
management has some mitigating influence, climate remains the dominant driver of
interannual nutrient export variability. Our projections did not incorporate dynamic land-
use or management-change scenarios, such as those from ISIMIP, which could alter long-
term nutrient inputs through conservation, cropping choices, or policy interventions. We
now note this as a source of uncertainty and recommend future work explicitly integrate
land-use and management scenarios alongside hydroclimate drivers to improve
projections. The revised text in the Methods section (lines 607-609) now reads: “This
regression assumes the historical relationship is primarily climate-driven and does not
explicitly account for potential long-term changes in agricultural practices or land use, which
we note as a source of uncertainty.”.
• Line 486: Why no Ecospace? And in Ecosim were environmental relationships used? [I can see
from the supplied model the answer is no, but please state this in the paper]
We thank the reviewer for this question. Our analysis was conducted in Ecosim rather than
Ecospace because our focus was on temporal dynamics at the scale of the entire Gulf of
Mexico ecosystem, for which spatially explicit modelling was not required. In Ecosim, we
did not include environmental response functions for individual functional groups, as our
objective was to assess the system’s response to drought forcing through changes in
nutrient input and primary productivity rather than to parameterize species-specific
environmental tolerances. We have now explicitly stated these points in the Methods
section for clarity. Future work may extend this analysis using Ecospace to examine the
spatiotemporal dynamics of drought impacts on the Gulf of Mexico ecosystem. We added a
note clarifying this point in the Methods section (lines 631-636) as follows: “Our analysis
was conducted in Ecosim rather than Ecospace because our focus was on temporal dynamics
at the scale of the entire GoM ecosystem, for which spatially explicit modelling was not
required. We also did not include species-specific environmental response functions; instead,
drought forcing was implemented through changes in nutrient input and primary productivity.
Future work may extend this approach with Ecospace to explore spatial heterogeneity.”.
• Line 505 “primary productivity anomaly”: Interaction with drought year reproduction?
We thank the reviewer for this observation. In our simulations, primary productivity
anomalies were applied as a proxy for the bottom-up effects of drought on the ecosystem,
but we did not explicitly model potential interactions with the timing of reproduction for
individual functional groups. We acknowledge that drought-induced changes in primary
productivity could overlap with spawning seasons or early life-history stages, thereby
amplifying recruitment impacts. Although Ecosim has the capability to incorporate
seasonal egg production forcing and can be used to test match–mismatch hypotheses,
these features were not implemented in the present study. We have now added a clarification
noting that phenological interactions were not explicitly represented here but could
influence recruitment dynamics, and should be incorporated in future work.
The revised section in the Discussion (lines 322-326) is as follows: “In addition, our
simulations used primary productivity anomalies as a proxy for drought forcing and did not
explicitly capture match–mismatch dynamics with spawning or recruitment; Ecosim can
incorporate seasonal egg production forcing, and future work should test such interactions to
better represent drought effects on early life stages.”.
• Line 533-534 “MEF values (see supplementary section S5, supplementary Table S5),
demonstrating the overall efficacy of the model”: Given the topic discussed here what was it for
menhaden and closely related species?
We thank the reviewer for this question. In the supplementary material (Table S5), the
model efficiency (MEF) values for Gulf menhaden were 0.65 (Age 1), 0.68 (Age 2), and 0.66
(Age 3), indicating good agreement between modelled and observed biomass trends across
age classes. For the most closely related functional groups, MEF values were 0.54 for
“Sardine–herring–scad” and 0.49 for “Mullet,” both reflecting reasonable skill in
reproducing historical dynamics. We have now added these specific values to the Results
section (lines 167-169) for clarity: “Notably, the model diagnostics indicated good skill
overall, with MEF values of 0.65–0.68 across Gulf menhaden age classes, and 0.54 and 0.49
for the closely related groups “Sardine–herring–scad” and “Mullet,” respectively (see
supplementary section S6, Table S5).”.
• Line 556-558 “The primary productivity and the free nutrient concentrations are linked through
a Michaelis-Menten uptake relationship, in which nutrient uptake increases asymptotically up to
a maximum in response to increasing free nutrient concentrations”: How exactly was it entered
into Ecosim? Straight primary productivity scalar or via an environmental response relationship
or ?
We thank the reviewer for this question. The Michaelis–Menten uptake relationship is an
internal feature of Ecosim’s primary producer dynamics and is not entered manually by
the user. In our simulations, free nutrient concentrations influenced primary productivity
through this built-in saturating uptake function, whereby nutrient-limited growth
increases asymptotically toward a maximum rate. This relationship operates automatically
within Ecosim based on the specified nutrient time series, ensuring that primary
productivity dynamically responds to modeled nutrient concentration changes over time.
We have updated the Methods (lines 694-698) section to clarify this point as follows: “The
base free nutrient proportion ,ensures that as producer biomass increases, free nutrient
availability declines and constrains further growth. The base free nutrient proportion was set
in our simulations to the default value of 0.5, provides the basis for the time-dependent
nutrient forcing, which is simulated using monthly multipliers of the Ecopath based nutrient
content estimate that represents the relative nutrient loading”.
• Line 559: Ecosim simulations: State the length of the simulation. Just the drought period or
longer? How long was the elevated F? Entire run just 5 years or are these periods layered into
longer runs? How is transitional change under directed forcing allowed for (background climate
driven shift)
We thank the reviewer for this question. For the historical simulations, we used actual
environmental and fishing data at yearly or monthly resolution, depending on availability.
For the projected 2050 and 2100 drought scenarios, nutrient input and fishing pressure
changes were applied over five consecutive years, with the terminal (fifth) year used for
analyses; the same approach was used for fishing pressure forcing. Transitional change
under directed forcing was represented by this five-year adjustment period, which
preliminary trials showed to be sufficient for the ecosystem to reach a new stable state
while remaining ecologically realistic and representative of isolated events. Background
climate variability was not included; instead, all projections used the mean conditions of
the last three years of the time series (geometric mean of 2014–2016) as the reference
baseline. We have updated the Methods section (lines 723-727) to clarify this point, as
follows: “All projected drought and fishing scenarios were implemented as isolated 5-year
simulations layered onto the 2014–2016 baseline conditions, with forcing applied throughout
the run and the terminal (fifth) year used for analyses. This design allowed transitional
dynamics under directed forcing to stabilize while remaining ecologically realistic.”
• Line 628 “purse seine effort”: How was this done? Or are you saying that is what the changing
F represents? Was it done via effort time series manipulation or F forcing?
We thank the reviewer for this question. In the simulations, both fishing mortality (F) and
purse-seine effort were implemented as forcing functions. For the scenarios, their values
were multiplied by the specified multipliers to represent changes in fishing pressure. We
added a note in the Methods section (lines: 727-731) clarifying this point as follows: “Both
Gulf menhaden fishing mortality (F) and purse-seine fleet effort were implemented as forcing
functions, with their values scaled by multipliers in the scenarios to reflect changes in fishing
pressure and associated technical interactions (e.g., bycatch). Background climate variability
beyond the applied drought and fishing scenarios was not included.”.
• Line 636-639 “These models, like others, encompass inherent uncertainty and are based on
assumptions or best available data concerning the species biology and life history. However, they
do represent the only source of absolute biomass for the entire GoM.”: We all do it, but not great
to condition a model with another model. Was there any cross check with data, like standardised
cpue or survey data etc?
We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. We acknowledge that conditioning
an ecosystem model with outputs from other models introduces additional assumptions and
uncertainties. In our case, not all biomass time series were model-based—many were
derived directly from observational datasets, including bottom trawl surveys and video-
based indices (Table S2). For certain groups, such as Gulf menhaden, absolute biomass
estimates were taken from available single-species assessment models due to the absence of
direct, fishery-independent absolute biomass measurements for the entire Gulf of Mexico.
Nevertheless, our analyses also incorporate fisheries-independent time series, including a
menhaden CPUE index based on abundance per trawl in Louisiana estuaries—the main
nursery area for Gulf menhaden—collected routinely by the Louisiana Department of
Wildlife and Fisheries (LDWF) (Section S3). These data, together with standardized CPUE
indices from the Gulf menhaden purse-seine fishery (adjusted for vessel, gear, and seasonal
effects; Berenshtein et al., 2021), were used to qualitatively check the consistency of
temporal patterns. While differences in spatial coverage, sampling design, and target
species composition precluded full quantitative validation, we now explicitly acknowledge
this limitation in the revised manuscript and recommend future integration of a broader
range of standardized observational datasets for cross-validation. We have updated the
Methods (Model limitations) section (lines 799-804) accordingly, as follows: “To partially
address this limitation, we cross-checked temporal trends against independent observational
datasets, including standardized CPUE indices from the Gulf menhaden purse-seine fishery
and fisheries-independent trawl-based juvenile abundance indices from Louisiana estuaries
(Section S3). While differences in design and coverage precluded full quantitative validation,
these comparisons provided qualitative consistency checks”.
• Line 652-653 “the positive contribution of nutrient input on fisheries production outweighs the
negative effect from hypoxic conditions.”: Yes but what happens in years with low inflow and
low nutrient input? Less hypoxia and related mortality along with the nutrient drop or is there a
lag so get hypoxia as well as the nutrient drop at least in the first year/s of the drought?
We thank the reviewer for this question. In our study, we did not explicitly model hypoxia
or its direct effects; instead, we referred to de Mutsert et al. (2016) to illustrate how
nutrient input changes can influence both primary production and hypoxic conditions. In
that study, hypoxic area was not simulated through a multi-year lag mechanism; rather, it
was linked directly to annual nutrient loading in the same year using empirically derived
relationships within the coupled physical–biological hypoxia model of Fennel et al. (2011),
which provided dissolved oxygen and chlorophyll-a values for each model cell at each time
step. As such, in years with low inflow and nutrient input, their model produced both
reduced primary production and reduced hypoxic area within that year, without an
explicit carryover of hypoxia from prior years. In addition, the empirical data on hypoxic
area presented in our study (Fig. S2e) show that, at the yearly scale, extreme declines in
hypoxic area (e.g., 1988, 2000, and 2012) were immediately associated with extreme
drought conditions, and that hypoxic area was restored once drought conditions
diminished. These results suggest that lagged effects are weak or absent. We have added a
clarifying comment on in the Methods (Model limitations) section (lines 819-828) as
follows: “Consistent with this, empirical data (Fig. S2e) show that hypoxic area declines
sharply during extreme drought years (e.g., 1988, 2000, 2012) and recovers once drought
conditions diminish, suggesting that lagged effects are weak or absent. Our simulations used
primary productivity anomalies as a proxy for drought forcing and did not explicitly capture
match–mismatch dynamics with spawning or recruitment. Ecosim can incorporate seasonal
egg production forcing, and future work should test such interactions to better represent
drought effects on early life stages. In addition, we did not explicitly incorporate salinity–
habitat interactions in our modeling framework. While salinity increases during droughts can
stress estuarine-dependent invertebrates (e.g., oysters, shrimp), the ecosystem-wide declines
observed here were reproduced based solely on nutrient forcing, supporting a parsimonious
focus on trophic mechanisms.”.

We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. We agree and have replaced “HMS” with

• Figure S2: Explain the period highlighted and why when highlighted drought period in the
main text figures. Also F (other than on 1 Yr olds) stayed high even as effort dropped. Why and
what does that mean for signature assumed into bycatch species in the runs?
We thank the reviewer for these observations. In Figure S2 (now Figure S3), the
highlighted period corresponds to the time period which was affected by the late 1980s
prolonged drought, which is the historical drought event analyzed in detail in the main
text. Regarding the observation that fishing mortality (F) for age classes other than 1-year-
olds remained high even as effort declined, this reflects the age-structured nature of the
single-species assessment outputs used to inform our model. Specifically, older age classes
may experience sustained fishing mortality due to their continued vulnerability to the
fishery, even when overall effort is reduced, because catch composition and selectivity
patterns disproportionately target these cohorts. It is also possible that F remained elevated
because drought-driven biomass reductions (lower denominator in F = C/B) amplified the
estimated mortality rates. In the context of our simulations, this means that for bycatch
species linked to menhaden fishing, the modelled signature of fishing pressure is still
influenced by these higher F values on older age classes, even when total effort is lower. We
have added clarifying text in the supplementary materials to explain the highlighted period
(lines 101-102, 111-112) as follows: “Shaded area represents the time period which was
affected by the late 1980s prolonged drought.”.
We have also added a note clarifying the implications of the F–effort relationship for
bycatch species assumptions (lines 79-83) as follows: “The apparent persistence of high F
despite declining effort likely reflects two processes: (i) the age-structured nature of the
assessment outputs, where older cohorts remain selectively targeted even under reduced effort;
and (ii) drought-driven reductions in biomass, which amplify the ratio of catch to biomass (F
= C/B), thereby inflating estimated mortality rates.”.
• Supplementary materials “While the dynamics of the post-1990 years align with the
expectation that as biomass increases, fishing effort should decrease, and vice versa, the
dynamics during the 1980s appear counterintuitive, as biomass decreased in parallel with a
decrease in fishing effort, supporting the dominance of an external environmental force such as
nutrient input deficiency.”: Could this be a case of effort reduction in response to biomass drop, so
start high together and then effort reduced in response to drop in biomass, with effort
reduction continuing on into later period where stocks then rebuilt?
We thank the reviewer for this insightful interpretation. The 1980s pattern may indeed
reflect a lagged management or economic response, with high initial effort reduced
following biomass declines and continuing to drop as stocks rebuilt. This aligns with our
proposed mechanism in which drought reduced biomass, leading to lower catches and
modest effort reductions. We have noted this explanation in the supplementary materials
(lines 126-128) as follows: “This pattern may also reflect a lagged management or economic
response, where effort initially remained high, then dropped in reaction to declining biomass,
and continued to decrease into the subsequent period as stocks rebuilt.”.

predicted biomass”: Plots possible so reader gets a sense of what this looks like?
We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. Plots comparing observed and model-predicted
biomass for key functional groups are already presented in detail in Berenshtein et al.,
2021, 2023, where model calibration and validation are described extensively. To
strengthen the current manuscript, we have added clarifying text in the supplementary
materials (Section S6, lines 169-172) explicitly directing readers to these sources, and we
emphasize that these figures demonstrate good agreement between modeled and observed
biomass dynamics, as follows: “For detailed plots comparing observed vs. model-predicted
biomass for key functional groups, see Berenshtein et al. (2021, 2023), where calibration and
validation are presented extensively. These figures visually illustrate the quality of model fit
and support the MEF values reported here.”.
• Supplementary materials “model predicted estimates of the fishing mortality rate corresponding
to the maximum sustainable yield (FMSY) and FMSY estimates from stock assessments.”:
Estimated in Ecosim/Ecopath how? Multiple ways this can be done.
We thank the reviewer for this question. In our analysis, F was estimated directly
MSY
within Ecosim using the compensatory MSY search routine. This procedure incrementally
adjusts fishing mortality rates for each functional group while holding other parameters
constant, to identify the rate that maximizes long-term equilibrium yield. The resulting
F values were then compared with independent estimates from single-species stock
MSY
assessments, as reported in the supplementary materials. We have added this explanation
to Supplementary Section S6 (lines 166-168) to clarify our approach as follows: “Ecosim-
derived Fₘₛᵧ values was estimated within Ecosim using the built-in equilibrium MSY
(compensatory) search routine, which iteratively adjusts fishing mortality to identify the rate

• Supplementary materials “As noted in the main text, the relative impact of fishing mortality
diminishes as drought-related effects on biomass intensify.”: As F not effort so catch drops in
step with productivity? Any consideration of whether could become synergistic if lag in F
response? Also bigger cumulative effect if rate of F in place longer before drought hits? Also
date of model base F vs 1988 F?
We thank the reviewer for these insightful points. In our model, fishing pressure was
applied as F (fishing mortality rate) and purse menhaden fleet effort, so catches varied
proportionally with changes in productivity and biomass. We did not explicitly model
synergistic effects from a lagged F response; however, we acknowledge that in reality,
delayed reductions in F could intensify biomass declines during drought. Similarly, higher
pre-drought F sustained over a longer period could produce larger cumulative impacts
when a drought occurs. The model’s baseline F values were taken from the EwE last
hidcast years (2014-2016), whereas the historical 1988 drought scenario used observed
fishing mortality rates from that period. We have added a note on this in the
supplementary materials (lines 172-179) as follows: “Note that our simulations applied both
fishing mortality (F) and purse-seine fleet effort, such that catches varied proportionally with
biomass and productivity. While this approach captures the relative impact of fishing under
drought forcing, it does not account for possible synergistic effects if reductions in F lag
behind biomass declines. In reality, such delays could intensify stock depletion, particularly
under extreme drought conditions. Likewise, sustained high F in the years preceding drought
events could produce stronger cumulative impacts once drought occurs. These potential
interactions were not explicitly represented here and should be explored in future model
extensions.”.
