review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

A major depletion of ~42% in total fisheries production occurred in the Gulf of Mexico in the early 1990’s but received limited scientific attention. Here, we show that terrestrial drought in the US during the late 1980s, combined with high Gulf menhaden (Brevoortia patronus) fishing pressure, led to a depleted forage base, with cascading effects on other species and fisheries in the Gulf, acting primarily via a reduction in Mississippi River flow. Ecosystem model simulations support these findings, and more importantly, indicate that anticipated frequent and intense drought conditions under the RCP 8.5 scenario in the US are projected to cause periodic depletions of biomass and catches of ~61% by 2050, and ~72% by 2100, substantially more acute than previous estimates for the Gulf. There is an urgent need to explore possible mitigation strategies and the mechanisms by which drought conditions affect the Gulf and other marine ecosystems.

---

## Introduction

The Gulf of Mexico (GoM) harbors a great wealth of natural resources including diverse ecosystems and productive fisheries1. The GoM ecosystem is nutrient-limited2, with more than 90% of GoM nutrient input supplied by the Mississippi River3. This nutrient input results in extensive primary productivity in the estuarine, coastal, and shelf regions of the GoM, supporting the growth of phytoplankton, seagrass, and algae that, along with detrital sources, serve as the trophic foundation for the GoM ecosystem4–6.

Within this system, Gulf menhaden (Brevoortia patronus) is the main forage fish, consisting of the largest harvested fish stock in the GoM by weight1. The Gulf menhaden represents an important trophic link between primary and secondary producers, i.e., phytoplankton and zooplankton, and multiple groups of higher trophic predators such as marine mammals, sharks, and mackerels7,8.

Numerous studies have highlighted the significant relationship between Gulf menhaden population dynamics and environmental conditions such as temperature, wind, and river flow9–11. While some research shows that wet conditions and high river flow positively affect Gulf menhaden recruitment, other findings indicate that excessive river flows can hinder recruitment due to increased larval offshore transport and predation12,13. This contradiction emphasizes the complex, scale-dependent interactions between these abiotic factors. Decadal analyses reveal a positive correlation between higher average river discharge and enhanced recruitment, likely driven by increased nutrient input and primary productivity13. Additionally, interannual climate oscillations, such as the Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation (AMO), North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO), and El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO), further complicate these dynamics. Beyond recruitment, research indicates that spring river discharge and winter ENSO conditions significantly influence menhaden oil content, a critical indicator of individual and population health, while fishing pressure and environmental conditions also exert contrasting effects on menhaden growth14.

River flow has long been recognized as a master variable regulating marine and estuarine ecosystems, influencing habitat availability, trophic dynamics, and fishers’ harvesting behavior15–19. Variability in river discharge controls nutrient delivery, sediment transport, and salinity gradients, all of which shape the productivity and distribution of marine organisms. In the GoM, a system otherwise strongly oligotrophic with limited nutrient input from oceanic currents or upwelling, riverine nutrient inputs are especially critical for sustaining fisheries yields20. This highlights a trophic-driven mechanism by which drought-induced reductions in river flow limit nutrient availability, cascading through the food web to affect forage fish, predators, fish migration and composition, and ultimately fisheries production.

The GoM fisheries are characterized by fluctuations in biomass and catches1. A notable decline occurred during the late 1980s and early 1990s1. During this period, cumulative biomass declined by 42% and cumulative catch by 34% relative to the 1982–1986 reference period, highlighting the severity of this system-wide depletion. The decline was evident in catches and biomass of a wide range of taxa including benthic primary producers, shrimp, oysters and crab, Gulf menhaden, cephalopods, as well as predators such as amberjack, cobia, king mackerel and Spanish mackerel1,21–23. Despite these wide systematic declines, limited attention has been given to their full scope of possible drivers and underlying mechanisms.

Prior to these declines, a severe and prolonged drought took place in the US, with increasingly dry conditions beginning in 1986 peaking in 1988, and ending in 1989. This drought caused damage of nearly 60 billion US$, resulting in massive agricultural losses, extensive wildfires, and severe interferences of barge transportation on the Mississippi River24. This severe drought resulted in a reduction of more than 50% in the Mississippi River flow and nutrient input to the GoM during summer months between 1985 and 198825.

Previous evidence shows that terrestrial drought significantly impacts fisheries collapse through hydrological, ecological, and socioeconomic mechanisms. Drought-related freshwater reductions elevate salinity, stressing taxa like oysters (Crassostrea virginica) and shrimp in GoM systems26–30. Sustained elevated salinity levels (>25 ppt) are linked to oyster mortality and recruitment failures27,28,30. In this study, we focus on the trophic pathway for three main reasons. First, nutrient-driven productivity is widely recognized as the dominant mechanism linking river flow to fisheries in this oligotrophic system, where oceanic nutrient supplies from upwelling or currents are limited. Second, our analytical framework is designed to represent trophic interactions at the ecosystem scale, rather than species-specific habitat–salinity responses. Third, the available long-term data are most consistent for nutrient inputs and productivity signals, making them more suitable for quantitative analysis.

Drought conditions and reduced river flow may influence the GoM ecosystem through the reduction of food web productivity via the reduction of nutrient input into the GoM through the Mississippi delta, around which the bulk of GoM fishery landings are harvested31. Based on this, we examine the connection between the drought-related nutrient input conditions and the subsequent declines in catch and biomass during the late 1980s; next, given the high probability of multi-decadal severe drought (megadrought) during the second half of the century32,33, we examine how multi-year extreme drought conditions anticipated in the Mississippi River basin during the 21st century may affect the GoM ecosystem using a trophic-dynamic ecosystem model. Specifically, we examine how biomass and catch in the GoM may respond to anticipated drought-related changes in the Mississippi River nutrient input to the GoM and compare drought-related impacts to those associated with increased fishing pressure on Gulf menhaden-the largest harvested fish stock in the GoM34.

---

## Results

Analyses of historical time series of environmental data indicate a drying trend in the Mississippi River basin, starting in 1985 and peaking in 1988, and hitting record low Palmer’s Drought Severity Index (PDSI; a standard measure of drought intensity35) annual and summer levels of −3.3 and −4.1, respectively (Fig. 1a). As a result, the Mississippi River level at Vicksburg, Mississippi (MS) declined to record low annual and summer levels of 12.2 and 3.2 ft, respectively (Fig. 1b). Similarly, the nutrient load from the Mississippi River to the GoM reached a record low annual and summer value of 107,717 and 41,560 t, respectively (Fig. 1c). For these three variables, the year 1988 is characterized by exceptionally low summer values compared to the rest of the years (Fig. 1e–g). Sea surface temperature (SST) anomaly and hypoxic areas were relatively low during the years 1985-1988 compared to the rest of the years (Fig. 1d, h, Fig. S2). The number of named hurricanes, which did not show correspondence to the other environmental factors, are provided in Fig. S2.

Analysis of historical fisheries data indicates a loss of 42% in cumulative biomass (i.e., aggregate biomass summed across all functional groups) and 34% in cumulative catch during the periods of 1988–1992 compared to 1982–1986. This trend is dominated by Gulf menhaden, which represents the bulk of the biomass and catch, and shows declines of 43% and 38%, respectively (Fig. 1i, j). Importantly, aside from the sharp drought-related reductions in PDSI, river discharge, and nutrient inputs in 1988, other environmental indicators (e.g., SST anomalies) and overall fishing effort levels were broadly comparable between the two periods (Fig. 1, Fig. S2), supporting the interpretation that the observed declines primarily reflect the drought effect. Within this broader stability, the menhaden purse-seine fleet did show a 16% reduction in relative effort (Fig. 1k), though this has been attributed to decreases in fleet size and processing capacity, driven by corporate acquisitions, downsizing, and industrial consolidation, rather than improvements in efficiency or changes in fishing pressure36. Additional menhaden related time series, including number of recruits, and an abundance index for juveniles based on fisheries-independent data collected routinely in Louisiana estuaries corroborate these results by showing low juvenile abundances from 1985 to 1991 (Fig. S3).

The declining trend during and following the drought period is not limited to Gulf menhaden and is evident in biomass depletion in 40 out of 45 functional groups (89%; Fig. 1l), and for catches, depletion in 30 out of 47 functional groups (63%; Fig. 1m). Groups exhibiting depletion include coastal invertebrate feeders (e.g., croakers (Sciaenidae)) and crabs, whereas groups that indicated a slight increase in biomass include reef piscivores (e.g., moray eels (Muraenidae)) and cobia (Fig. 1l). Depletion in catch was strongest in large coastal sharks. The largest increase in catches over that period occurred in sandbar shark and gray triggerfish (Fig. 1m).

PDSI projections based on the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project 5 (CMIP5) model ensembles for the Mississippi River basin33 indicate that prolonged (5 yrs) drought conditions anticipated by 2050 are expected to reach a PDSI value of -3.88 (Fig. 2a), and prolonged drought conditions anticipated for 2051–2100 are expected to be more severe, reaching a low PDSI value of -5.66. The extreme drought events documented during our historical period, correspond in values to the lower 5 percentile range of the CMIP5 model ensembles (Fig. 2a). The gradual decrease in PDSI across time indicates an increasing probability and severity of prolonged extreme drought periods, in particular in the western and central regions of the Mississippi River basin (Fig. 2a). The drought conditions anticipated by 2050 and during 2051–2100 will be manifested as reductions in nutrient inputs to the GoM by factors of 0.57 and 0.45, respectively, based on the linear relationship between the two variables (Linear regression, p < 0.0001, F = 53.5, R2 = 0.6, Nut = 1.09 + 0.09 × PDSI, Fig. 2b).

Results indicate that the biomass and catch of Gulf menhaden are strongly affected by variability in nutrient input to the GoM, and by the fishing mortality of Gulf menhaden (Fig. 2c). Assuming no change in Gulf menhaden fishing mortality from the status quo, the model projection indicates that extreme drought conditions anticipated by 2050 will result in an approximate reduction of 61% of total biomass and catch compared to the status quo projection (Fig. 2c); whereas for drought conditions anticipated at the end of the 21st century, biomass and catch reduction could be reduced by as much as 72% (Fig. 2c). The effect of Gulf menhaden fishing mortality on the cumulative biomass and catch dynamics is smaller compared to the effect of anticipated droughts (Fig. 2c), suggesting that the ability of the ecosystem to compensate for menhaden harvest is compromised under drought conditions. This reduced influence of fishing mortality reflects the strong bottom-up limitation imposed by nutrient input, whereby menhaden biomass remains low even when fishing mortality (F) is set to 0, and compensatory mechanisms prevent collapse at low stock sizes. As a result, absolute removals and the ecosystem-level footprint of fishing diminish relative to the dominant drought effect. Notably, the model diagnostics indicated good skill overall, with MEF values of 0.65–0.68 across Gulf menhaden age classes, and 0.54 and 0.49 for the closely related groups Sardine–herring–scad and Mullet, respectively (see supplementary note S4, Table S5).

The model demonstrated that Gulf menhaden (Fig. 2d) and its predators, such as king (Fig. 2e) and Spanish (Fig. 2f) mackerels, respond to Gulf menhaden biomass such that when Gulf menhaden biomass increases, the biomass of its predators increases respectively, and vice-versa (Fig. 2d–f). Droughts during the 21st century, through the reduction of nutrient input to marine environment, are expected to result in drastic declines in biomass and catches of the Gulf menhaden and its associated predators, with a decreasing effect of the Gulf menhaden fishing mortality with increasing drought conditions (Fig. 2d–f).

For status quo nutrient input and increased (x2) Gulf menhaden fishing mortality conditions, corresponding to the maximum value observed historically (1980–2016 relative to 2016), there is a decrease in the biomass of several groups: Gulf menhaden, their associated predators, species that are bycatch in the menhaden purse seine fleet (e.g., seatrout), and other species that decline due to indirect trophic interactions. In contrast, the biomass of the competitors of these groups (e.g., cephalopods), increases (Fig. 3a). In conditions of reduced nutrient input anticipated for 2100 drought conditions, the biomasses of all groups are depleted, with a more marked effect on lower trophic species such as Gulf menhaden and shrimp (Fig. 3b). At the functional-group level, projections show that drought impacts are not uniform (Fig. 3b). Lower trophic levels, including benthic invertebrates, reef-associated species, and juvenile menhaden and Spanish mackerel, experience the strongest biomass reductions, consistent with bottom-up nutrient limitation. In contrast, some higher trophic-level piscivores (e.g., billfish, cobia, other tunas) show milder responses. These results highlight an overall contraction at the base and mid-levels of the food web, with heterogeneous responses among top predators. These dynamics explicitly account for technical interactions, as fleets in the model are linked to multiple functional groups through both targeted catch and bycatch based on observed composition and selectivity.

---

## Methods

Historical analysis
The time period addressed in our historical analysis is 1980–2016. The start year was chosen due to data availability, as many biological sampling programs in the GoM were initiated at that time and most fisheries stock assessments characterize population dynamics from the 1980s. Time series with fewer than four years of missing data were used for the cumulative biomass and catch analyses. Biomass time series used for the cumulative time series plot (Fig. 1) include only SouthEast Data Assessment and Review (SEDAR) assessed groups (N=12), as these derived quantities were estimated by population dynamics models and accepted for use by fisheries experts. Only time series with two or less missing data points between 1980-1992 (the focal historical period) were used for this analysis. Missing data in biomass and catch time series were replaced with the geometric mean of the four adjacent values in the time series, i.e., two before and two after the missing value. If missing values were at the edges of the time series, i.e., t1, t2, tend-1, tend, available adjacent values were used. For example, if t1 was missing, it was replaced with the geometric mean of t2, t3, and t4. For computing the relative change between pre-drought and drought affected years we compared 1982–1986 and 1988–1992 at the group level. Only time series without missing data for these periods were used, which included data derived from SEDAR assessments, Gulf Data Assessment and Review (GDAR) assessments, SouthEast Area Monitoring and Assessment Program (SEAMAP) trawl surveys, and the pelagic observer program. Following data filtering, computations of cumulative biomass were conducted for the following species: blacktip, dusky, and sandbar sharks; large and small coastal sharks; greater amberjack; cobia; king mackerel (ages 0–1 and 1–2 years); Spanish mackerel (ages 0–1 and 1–2 years); gag and yellowedge groupers (0–3 and >3 years); goliath grouper; red snapper (0–1, 1–2, and >3 years); vermilion and mutton snappers; tilefish; gray triggerfish; and menhaden (1–2, 2–3, 3–4, and >4 years). Two missing data points (blacktip shark and mutton snapper in 1980) were addressed using geometric mean interpolation.

For assessed species, time series of commercial and recreational catches were obtained directly from the stock assessment output files (Table S2). For the remaining species, time series of catches were obtained by combining commercial fisheries landings with recreational landings from the Marine Recreational Information Program (MRIP), Southeast Region Headboat Survey (SRHS), and the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department (TPWD). Retained bycatch in the menhaden purse seine fishery was also included within the catch time series to capture removals of non-target species from the ecosystem (for more details see Table 9 in Berenshtein et al.6. Discards for other fisheries were not incorporated into catch time series.

We used catch rather than catch-per-unit-effort (CPUE) because our goal was to evaluate total fisheries production across the ecosystem, not standardized catch rates. Catch reflects the total biomass removed, making it directly comparable across functional groups, whereas CPUE data were inconsistent in availability, standardization, and coverage. Where available (e.g., Gulf menhaden), CPUE indices were used qualitatively to validate biomass patterns but not as dependent variables. Time series of commercial fishing effort by fleet and recreational fishing effort by mode (private boat, charter boat, headboat, and shore) were obtained from stock assessment documents when possible (Table S3). For the remaining commercial fishing fleets, time series of commercial effort were obtained from the National Marine Fisheries Service Vessel Operating Units (NMFS VOU) database59, which provides general trends in fishing effort dynamics (in terms of number of vessels or gear fished). Recreational fishing-effort time series (number of angler trips) were obtained from MRIP, SRHS, and TPWD (Table S3).

Environmental variables were downloaded from national and federal databases on a monthly resolution for the years 1980–2016. For measuring the degree of drought severity, we used the Palmer’s Drought Severity Index (PDSI)1, which is a drought index calculating soil moisture balance from inputs of precipitation and evapotranspiration. Mississippi basin PDSI was obtained from the National Centers for Environmental Information60 for the divisional region of the Mississippi River Basin & Tributaries (division code #220). Mississippi River level (ft) was obtained from the US army corps of engineers database61 for the Mississippi River gauge at Vicksburg, MS (32.312500N 90.906944W). Mississippi monthly nutrient loads (total nitrogen plus total phosphorus) data were obtained from the US Geological Survey25. Sea surface temperature was downloaded from the database of the GoM ecosystem status report1, which utilized data from daily high-resolution blended analysis for sea surface temperature62. Additional time series of named hurricanes, hypoxic area, and additional Gulf menhaden-related variables are provided in the extended time series section in supplementary note S1.

PDSI and Nutrient input projections until 2100 based on future scenario (RCP 8.5)
PDSI projections are based on the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project 5 (CMIP5) model output computed in Cook et al.,33, which were part of the Fifth Assessment Report (AR5) of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC). We focus on RCP 8.5-high emissions scenario (i.e., Representative Concentration Pathways resulting in a radiative forcing of 8.5 W/m2 at the end of the century)63. The calibration period for the PDSI calculations was 1931–1990. Potential evapotranspiration (PET) for the PDSI projections28 was computed based on the Penman-Monteith method64. The monthly PDSI values of each of the CMIP5 models (Table S4) were averaged spatially across all grid cells that are located within the Mississippi River basin65, based on horizontal resolution of 1.25o (Longitude) x 0.94o (Latitude). Specific PDSI values that are expected to represent prolonged droughts in the first and the second halves of the 21st century, were computed as the minimum mean PDSI value in a moving average window of five years for the periods of 2017-2050 and 2051–2100, respectively. MATLAB 2020b was used for all spatial and temporal analyses of the PDSI projections data. To project future nutrient input under drought conditions, we used linear least squares regression to model the relationship between historical nutrient input and the Palmer Drought Severity Index. This regression assumes the historical relationship is primarily climate-driven and does not explicitly account for potential long-term changes in agricultural practices or land use, which we note as a source of uncertainty. To ensure the assumptions of this linear regression were met, we assessed the normality of the residuals using a Q-Q plot and the Shapiro-Wilk test (p = 0.8), confirming normality and validating the statistical approach. The resulting regression equation was then used to estimate nutrient inputs for the first and second halves of the 21st century under projected drought conditions.

This study utilized CMIP5 PDSI projections for future drought scenarios due to data availability. However, recent CMIP6 projections indicate even more severe drought conditions for the Mississippi River basin65. While both CMIP5 and CMIP6 project drying trends, CMIP6 models show more extensive and severe drying in the Mississippi River basin region. Therefore, our CMIP5-based results likely represent a conservative estimate of future drought impacts (supplementary note S3).

Ecosystem modeling: Ecopath and Ecosim (EwE) analysis and data sources
We used the US Gulf-wide Ecopath with Ecosim (EwE) model4,6 to examine the possible effects of variability in nutrient input and Gulf menhaden fishing mortality on the GoM ecosystem. EwE66 is an ecosystem modeling framework that is widely used for exploring ecosystem trophic dynamics, and the effect of environmental and anthropogenic stressors on the ecosystem, namely fishing pressure. The modeling framework is based on two main components: (1) Ecopath, a static mass-balanced snapshot representing the ecosystem’s food web and static trophic interactions66 and (2) Ecosim, a temporal-dynamic model expressed through a series of differential equations simulating ecosystem dynamics over time67. Our analysis was conducted in Ecosim rather than Ecospace because our focus was on temporal dynamics at the scale of the entire GoM ecosystem, for which spatially explicit modelling was not required. We also did not include species-specific environmental response functions; instead, drought forcing was implemented through changes in nutrient input and primary productivity. Future work may extend this approach with Ecospace to explore spatial heterogeneity.

The model area represents all state and federal waters of the US GoM continental shelf and coastline (down to a bottom depth of ~400 m). The GoM food web model includes 78 trophic groups, including three marine mammal groups, separate aggregate groups for seabirds and sea turtles, eight elasmobranch groups, 52 fish groups, 18 of which are partitioned into multiple life stages, nine invertebrate groups, three primary producers, and one detritus group (supplementary Table S1). Twelve commercial fishing fleets are modeled based on gear and/or targeted species (bottom trawl (shrimp), bottom trawl (other), purse seine (menhaden), purse seine (other), pots and traps, handline, dredge, nets, pelagic longline, reef fish longline, shark longline, and other), and four recreational fleets include private angling, charter, headboat, and shore (supplementary Table S3).

In Berenshtein et al.6 and in Berenshtein et al.5 there is further description of data inputs, assumptions required for model development, model outputs, results and key system characteristics related to fisheries dynamics, biomass flow, ecological indices, and network analysis. Note that the difference between the model version used in the current study and that described in Berenshtein et al.6 is the estimation of the last year of the hindcast modeled period (2016) of the primary productivity anomaly time series. The primary productivity anomaly is computed as part of the automatic Ecosim fitting routine and is based on an iterative search algorithm which minimizes the errors’ sum of squares with respect to the reference time series5. The default estimation of the search algorithm for 2016 was unrealistically high because there was no subsequent year information to constrain this estimate. This would have generated biased estimations of the other groups biomasses for the last year of the hindcast modeled period (2016). Hence in the current version, the last year was not estimated and was set to the default value of one (i.e. no primary productivity anomaly).

The Ecosim model’s calibration employed 109 time series of biomass and landings (1980–2016) from stock assessments and monitoring surveys. While the model effectively represented economically important species with robust data (e.g., amberjack, Spanish mackerel), its accuracy diminished for data-poor and highly migratory species, reflecting data limitations and uncertainties. Model performance, as part of the fitting procedure described in Berenshtein et al.6, was assessed based on the sum-of-squared errors (SSE). Model diagnostics indicate good agreement between model predicted biomass with many reference time series and between model predicted estimates of the fishing mortality rate corresponding to the maximum sustainable yield (FMSY) and F estimates from stock assessments. Most cases of discrepancies between model and referenced data were for highly migratory species or data-poor species and likely result from data limitations or drivers not representative solely of the GoM6. In this study, we also evaluated performance across time series using modeling efficiency (MEF; supplementary note S4, supplementary Table S5), calculated as shown in Eq. 1:

MEF = 1 - Σ(Y^i - Yi)2 / Σ(Yi - Y_mean)2 (1)

This analysis indicated high MEF values for commercially important groups, including groupers, snappers, and mackerels. However, the model exhibited limitations in capturing high-frequency fluctuations in highly migratory species and younger age classes biomass. Despite these challenges, over 74% of the time series produced positive MEF values (see supplementary note S4, supplementary Table S5), demonstrating the overall efficacy of the model.

Nutrient input and primary production in EwE
Ecosim accounts for bottom-up drivers on primary production using a Michaelis-Menten nutrient uptake model. Specifically, the EwE modeling framework assumes that the total nutrient concentration can be divided between that which is available (free) and unavailable for uptake (e.g., bound in biomass). The total nutrient content is computed as the ratio between the total nutrient inflow rate from all nutrient loading sources, and the total loss rate considering all loss pathways (e.g., advection, sedimentation, and harvest). The Ecopath base estimate of total nutrient concentration is calculated by the EwE software based on the biomass pool value, its fixed nutrient content per unit of biomass pool, and the free nutrient concentration68.

The base free nutrient proportion ensures that as producer biomass increases, free nutrient availability declines and constrains further growth. The base free nutrient proportion was set in our simulations to the default value of 0.5, provides the basis for the time-dependent nutrient forcing, which is simulated using monthly multipliers of the Ecopath based nutrient content estimate that represents the relative nutrient loading. Here, nutrient loading, inputted as a forcing function time series, is represented by total monthly nitrogen and phosphorus input from the Mississippi River (t), scaled by the mean of the entire time period. such that:

Ni = Pi * (Nitrogenloadi + Phosphorosloadi) / (Nitrogenload_mean + Phosphorosload_mean) (2)

Where i is a given month and n is the total number of months in the hindcast modeled period (N=444). In each simulation, the free and bound nutrient fractions must sum to the total nutrient content, which results in a depletion of free nutrients under conditions of increased growth, limiting primary productivity. The primary productivity and the free nutrient concentrations are linked through a Michaelis-Menten uptake relationship, in which nutrient uptake increases asymptotically up to a maximum in response to increasing free nutrient concentrations68.

Ecosim simulations
Four types of simulations were conducted (Table S6). First, Biomass and catches comparison hindcast + projections: main runs (33 runs) examined functional group biomass and catch under varying nutrient input and fishing pressure levels for historical (1980s drought) and projected (2050, 2100) drought scenarios. Second, Biomass and catches comparison hindcast + projections: error bars (258 runs) calculated the standard deviation in biomass and catch based on the uncertainty of the CMIP5 climate projections used, derived from the 5th confidence interval percentile of the CMIP5 PDSI projections. Third, Biomass and catches comparison: tradeoff analysis (231 runs) assessed biomass and catch across a range of nutrient input and menhaden fishing pressure multipliers to investigate trade-offs between these factors. Finally, Sensitivity analysis of number of drought years (66 runs) evaluated the influence of drought duration (1-year vs. 3-year droughts) on the ecosystem under projected future climate conditions (supplementary note S5, Fig. S5). All projected drought and fishing scenarios were implemented as isolated 5-year simulations layered onto the 2014–2016 baseline conditions, with forcing applied throughout the run and the terminal (fifth) year used for analyses. This design allowed transitional dynamics under directed forcing to stabilize while remaining ecologically realistic. Both Gulf menhaden fishing mortality (F) and purse-seine fleet effort were implemented as forcing functions, with their values scaled by multipliers in the scenarios to reflect changes in fishing pressure and associated technical interactions (e.g., bycatch). Background climate variability beyond the applied drought and fishing scenarios was not included.

Quantifying changes in biomass and catches
We assessed changes in biomass and catches in response to historical and future drought conditions through a series of analyses. We chose to focus on Gulf menhaden due to its significant economic and ecological role in the GoM. This forage fish supports the largest fishery in the region by weight, serving as a crucial trophic link between phytoplankton, zooplankton, and various higher trophic level predators, including king mackerel, Spanish mackerel, and seatrout.

Historical perspective. We examined the differences between pre-drought conditions (1982–1986) and drought-affected conditions (1988–1992) using both historical time series data (Fig. 1l, m) and EwE time-dynamic Ecosim Model simulations (Fig. 2c). This involved analyzing input time series data (for sources, see Tables S1-3). Specifically, we compared the averages of the biomass and catches of the historical (H) time series data for these two distinct periods using the following (Eq. 3)

relative biomass change H = (B 1988-1992 - B 1982-1986) / (B 1988-1992 + B 1982-1986) (3)

This formulation bounds the relative change between -1 and 1, with a value of 0 indicating no change.

Future perspective. For the future analysis, we quantify changes in biomass and catches in response to projected drought conditions while accounting for varying levels of Gulf menhaden fishing mortality, conducting a trade-off analysis similar to the methodologies employed in Chagaris et al.69, and in Berenshtein et al.5. This approach is conceptually similar to methodologies for assessing potential climate change impacts in other ecosystems, such as temperature or zooplankton effects on the productivity of Ecosim models70.

We simulated a drought length of five years, a duration considered realistic given the anticipated increase in both the severity and frequency of droughts in the 21st century32. To model nutrient input under prolonged drought conditions, we implemented two specific nutrient values anticipated for the first and second halves of the century. Projected nutrient inputs were calculated using a least squares linear regression between the EwE Mississippi nutrient forcing and the Palmer Drought Severity Index (PDSI) in the Mississippi River basin. The resulting future nutrient input values were derived from this regression equation (Fig. 2a, b).

For each projection scenario, the terminal (fifth) year biomass was expressed relative to the terminal biomass of the status quo scenario, where nutrient and fishing conditions were set based on the geometric mean of the last three years of the US Gulf-wide EwE model (2014–2016). This relationship is articulated as:

B ratio = B T,sim / B T,statusquo (4)

where B T represents the terminal (fifth) year biomass from the climate scenario simulation and status quo projections.

To calculate the relative change in the projected biomass and catch for each group under future (F) scenarios, we used the following formula:

relative biomass change = (B F T,sim - B T,statusquo) / (B F T,sim + B T,statusquo) (5)

This formulation bounds the relative change between -1 and 1, with a value of 0 indicating no change.

Finally, to explore the trade-offs between nutrient input and Gulf menhaden fishing mortality (Fig. 2d–f), we conducted a series of five-year projection scenarios. Nutrient load and fishing mortality were modeled based on the geometric mean of the last three terminal years (2014–2016), with multipliers for nutrient forcing ranging from 0 to 2 in increments of 0.1 (N=21), and for fishing mortality from 0 to 5 in increments of 0.5 (N=11), resulting in a total of 231 scenarios (11 x 21). This approach enabled the simultaneous manipulation of menhaden fishing mortality, purse seine effort, and nutrient input, thus incorporating the trophic effects of nutrient inputs and menhaden harvest on the GoM ecosystem.

Model limitations
While the historical and projected fisheries declines are robust and systematic across the entire trophic range, it is important to note the limitations and uncertainties of the referenced data and the modeling framework. For example, most groups’ biomass reference data are a product of stock assessment models, which consider processes such as age-specific natural mortality, growth, recruitment, and fishing mortality37. These models, like others, encompass inherent uncertainty and are based on assumptions or best available data concerning the species biology and life history. However, they do represent the only source of absolute biomass for the entire GoM. To partially address this limitation, we cross-checked temporal trends against independent observational datasets, including standardized CPUE indices from the Gulf menhaden purse-seine fishery and fisheries-independent trawl-based juvenile abundance indices from Louisiana estuaries (supplementary note S1). While differences in design and coverage precluded full quantitative validation, these comparisons provided qualitative consistency checks. In addition, assessment output data are smoothed relative to observed data, which may result in the loss of high frequency variability. On the other hand, the thorough revision of data and model outputs enhances quality control and mitigates unrealistic fluctuations that may arise from data derived from methods such as bottom trawl surveys71. Catch data also harbors uncertainties related to unreported or misreported catches, as well as uncertain estimations of recreational landings. Furthermore, factors unrelated to environmental conditions and fishing pressure, such as management regulations, can significantly influence population and ecosystem dynamics38.

Limitations of the US Gulf-wide EwE model include lack of consideration of spatially explicit processes such as migration or spatially explicit mortality, for example of harmful algal blooms and hypoxic zones. In our model, hypoxia was not explicitly implemented, partially because our domain is Gulf-wide, and the hypoxic zone is localized near the mouth of the Mississippi River. However, in a previous study57, a spatially explicit EwE model for the northern GoM implemented hypoxia as well as nutrient input72, and concluded that the positive contribution of nutrient input on fisheries production outweighs the negative effect from hypoxic conditions. Consistent with this, empirical data (Fig. S2e) show that hypoxic area declines sharply during extreme drought years (e.g., 1988, 2000, 2012) and recovers once drought conditions diminish, suggesting that lagged effects are weak or absent. Our simulations used primary productivity anomalies as a proxy for drought forcing and did not explicitly capture match–mismatch dynamics with spawning or recruitment. Ecosim can incorporate seasonal egg production forcing, and future work should test such interactions to better represent drought effects on early life stages. In addition, we did not explicitly incorporate salinity–habitat interactions in our modeling framework. While salinity increases during droughts can stress estuarine-dependent invertebrates (e.g., oysters, shrimp)19, the ecosystem-wide declines observed here were reproduced based solely on nutrient forcing, supporting a parsimonious focus on trophic mechanisms. Part of the uncertainty in our model is attributed to knowledge gaps with respect to the life history and traits of functional groups in the GoM ecosystem, limited diet (stomach content) data, as well as limited capacity in correct characterization of highly migratory species. In addition, limitations exist in the taxonomic resolution for marine mammals, seabirds, and turtles as well as in the limited time series available for model calibration for these groups. Nevertheless, the US Gulf-wide EwE model characterizes the diverse GoM ecosystem and incorporates extensive reference data (161 reference and forcing time series), many of which correspond well with model predictions6.

### Reviewer 1

This paper is a well written and timely evaluation of the impacts of climate change on future GoM ecosystem and fishery productivity. It is unique in the aspect that it connects climate impacts on land (drought) to those in marine systems via changes in freshwater nutrient inputs to GoM. This is an often postulated interaction (i.e., climate impacts on land and water will impact marine systems) but there is a paucity of published papers that demonstrate or evaluate the phenomenon. The authors use a combination of a nutrient-forced mass-balance ecosystem model (EwE) and mean future climate projections of a drought index (PDSI) from an ensemble of 20 General Circulation Models (GCMs) representing a subset of CMIP5 ensemble members under the high baseline Representative Carbon Pathway (RCP 8.5). The authors derived a linear relationship between historical nutrients and historical PDSI values and used the nutrient relationship to drive bottom up productivity changes in the EwE model. The authors then force the EwE model with profiles across ranges in nutrient changes (0 -2 fold 2014-2016 average nutrient levels) and ranges in fishing pressure (0-5 x average F from 2014-2016). This represents an innovative application of an approach that has been applied successfully to evaluate potential climate change impacts in other systems, albeit with different climate couplings (e.g., where temperature or zooplankton drive productivity of EwE models; sensu https://doi.org/10.1111/gcb.13471 ). In general this is the type of analysis that can be vital for risk assessments of climate change impacts on marine fisheries as well as cumulative impacts of changes on land on marine ecosystems. In general, I strongly support this type of approach, and applaud the authors for using an ecosystem model (which captures indirect and cascading impacts) to evaluate climate change impacts on marine species. This can be a more robust approach than a direct climate-linked single species modeling effort.
However, there are a number of fundamental issues with the paper that I believe preclude it from being published until it is revised. I hope the authors are able to correct and address these issues so it can be used to advance understanding of climate change risk to marine ecosystems and fisheries.
The largest concern I have is that the paper is predicated on a linkage between droughts and historical declines in GoM catches that the authors do not demonstrate and which is not supported by the cited peer-reviewed papers (nor by the large number of non-peer reviewed technical reports that are cited). The authors postulate that a long (~3 year) drought in the mid- to late 1980’s induced a decline in biomass and catch that is reflected in the timeseries for both. These are plotted in Figure 1 (a) (e) and (f). However, one quickly notes that there are similar large drops in the PDSI index in ~2000 and ~2012 but no similar subsequent drop in catch or biomass timeseries as was seen in the late 1980’s. In the discussion section (lines 160-172) the authors try to address this and explain it as a difference in drought length (3 yrs for the earlier drought versus ~1 year for the others) and timing. This section is very speculative, without any citations save for one at the end of the paragraph stating that the severity of the drought can be related to the contrast between preceding wet years. In fact the largest concern I had in reading this section was that there was no mention of possible changes in fishery management or markets that could also explain the decline in catch. Additionally, following the sharp drop in in both catches and biomass in the late 1980’s catches remain low while biomass increases, pointing towards a non-biomass driver of low catches (e.g., shift in management towards lower harvest mortality rates). Finally there are multiple disparate patterns in the magnitude and sometimes the direction of biomass change and catch (this can be seen in Fig 1 (h) and (i); e.g., crab have the second largest decline in biomass but increases in catch, similarly, younger menhaden had the larger declines in biomass than older conspecifics but declines in older menhaden catches were larger than younger ones). This is of course a not unexpected and well cited issue in fisheries, especially as biomass declines where fishers can increase effort to offset declining biomass, or where catch declines but is stabilized over time and biomass increases due to implementation of policies that reduce harvest rates to sustainable levels. I believe the authors are aware of this issue (see plots of relative effort) and offer what is maybe the most parsimonious explanation in the “model limitation” section of the Methods (lines 506 -509):
506 “...For example, fluctuations in Gulf menhaden catches may
507 be related to economic processes, which occurred during the mid and late 1980s, when the Gulf
508 menhaden fishery underwent corporate consolidation resulting in declines in the number of
509 fishing vessels and processing plants. This may have contributed to the decline in catches 45. For
510 species such as Goliath grouper, declines in biomass and catch are likely a result of long periods
511 of overfishing or management regulations designed to reduce harvest (e.g., harvest moratorium).”
Similarly, the ESR (reference #1) states “The Gulf of Mexico Fisheries Management Council implemented a number of Fishery Management Plans in the 1980s, and major Amendments restricting fishing effort were passed in the 1990s.“ (p22).
Of course these management measures could have been implemented to address the decline that was driven initially by drought. The way to address how much climate drove the decline is to run a hindcast or counterfactual simulation, although these are challenging with ecosystem models because of model drift. So another approach would be to use a sensitivity simulation to evaluate the hypothesis of prolonged drought versus short 1 year drought in driving declines. E.g., fixing the F rate at a few different levels (e.g., those observed in the 1985-1990 period vs those observed in 2013), simulate a) 3 year drought (sensu the 1985-1988) and b) a five year period with a 1 year drought. Something like this should be conducted to demonstrate and support the postulation that underlies the projection simulations. In the absence of the sensitivity simulation above, there is not sufficient evidence provided presently to rule out changes in harvest pressure, fisheries operations, management or markets in driving declines in catch in the late 1980’s relative to early 1980’s. Given that the paper is predicated on the postulated relationship between drought, nutrients, and declines in catches, establishing and supporting this is extremely important. Additionally, I strongly suggest providing a historical time-series of harvest mortality by age for menhaden (e.g., as a supplemental figure). It appears to my eye that the F rate for 1 year old fish is much higher during the 1985-1990 period than 2000 - 2016. Having the timeseries would help facilitate comparisons in relative fishing pressure over time..
The second issue with the paper is that it is very difficult to discern precisely what methods were used in the simulations. This needs to be clarified in the Methods simulation section. I have detailed a number of line by line suggestions below to help clarify. There were two separate simulations conducted. For the first, I believe the correct methods were used for the status quo versus future time series projections, but can’t confirm this based on the current methods section. For the second the authors used linear regression to extrapolate the nutrient levels from the PDSI projections for the first and second halves of the century.

This is important because ecosystem models can propagate error when adjusting to new forcings and including a control run helps establish that differences are due to forcings rather than model behavior. If this was done the authors need to clarify the start and end dates of each simulation and in figure and the results consistently use a term like “persistence simulation” or “control” rather than “2016” which is confusing. A table or figure of the simulation methodology would greatly help clarify the two simulations.
For the second simulation, it is not clear from the Methods which years are included in this extrapolation; values are reported in the Results section and Figure 2.b but again it is difficult to understand which years are included in the values as they are reported as “anticipated by 2050 and during 2051-2100). A growing number of papers include comparisons of projections of high and low carbon emission scenarios, e.g., RCP8.5 vs RCP2.6 or the more recent CMIP6 SSP126 vs SSP 585. These types of comparisons are extremely useful in IPCC and other climate assessments because they reveal the relative risk of different levels of greenhouse gas emissions. To repeat this analysis for RCP2.6 would be a major undertaking and so I am not suggesting that has to be done here, but including multiple carbon emission scenarios is something the authors might consider in future work as it would help address an important need for relative climate risk information for fisheries and marine ecosystems.

### Reviewer 2

In the ms by Berenshtein et al., the authors present data that indicates a severe drought in the southeast U.S., combined with fishing pressure on ecologically important menhaden in the Gulf of Mexico, likely caused a decline in marine food webs and fisheries catch in the 1980s. Using these results the authors modeled future fisheries in the GoM under simulated drought conditions. First, I would like to thank the authors for expanding the knowledge on the ecosystem dynamics of this region, and further exploring the role of freshwater/nutrient inputs in ocean ecosystems. I believe this could add to the growing body of knowledge to an important socio-ecological system. With that said, I believe there are too many confounding factors that could contribute to the lack of nutrients being the main driver to population dynamics in the region, and this would be important for informing a more robust predictive model, and thus should be considered before publication.

Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
This paper is a well written and timely evaluation of the impacts of climate change on future
GoM ecosystem and fishery productivity. It is unique in the aspect that it connects climate
impacts on land (drought) to those in marine systems via changes in freshwater nutrient inputs to
GoM. This is an often postulated interaction (i.e., climate impacts on land and water will impact
marine systems) but there is a paucity of published papers that demonstrate or evaluate the
phenomenon. The authors use a combination of a nutrient-forced mass-balance ecosystem model
(EwE) and mean future climate projections of a drought index (PDSI) from an ensemble of 20
General Circulation Models (GCMs) representing a subset of CMIP5 ensemble members under
the high baseline Representative Carbon Pathway (RCP 8.5). The authors derived a linear
relationship between historical nutrients and historical PDSI values and used the nutrient
relationship to drive bottom up productivity changes in the EwE model.
The authors then force the EwE model with profiles across ranges in nutrient changes (0 -2 fold
2014-2016 average nutrient levels) and ranges in fishing pressure (0-5 x average F from 2014-
2016). This represents an innovative application of an approach that has been applied
successfully to evaluate potential climate change impacts in other systems, albeit with different
climate couplings (e.g., where temperature or zooplankton drive productivity of EwE models;
sensu https://doi.org/10.1111/gcb.13471 ). In general this is the type of analysis that can be vital
for risk assessments of climate change impacts on marine fisheries as well as cumulative impacts
of changes on land on marine ecosystems. In general, I strongly support this type of approach,
and applaud the authors for using an ecosystem model (which captures indirect and cascading
impacts) to evaluate climate change impacts on marine species. This can be a more robust
approach than a direct climate-linked single species
modeling effort.
However, there are a number of fundamental issues with the paper that I believe preclude it from
being published until it is revised. I hope the authors are able to correct and address these issues
so it can be used to advance understanding of climate change risk to marine ecosystems and
fisheries.
We thank the reviewer for the positive comments. In the revised manuscript, we have
thoroughly addressed the concerns raised by incorporating additional analyses, integrating
new data, and expanding the relevant sections as needed. We have also included the
citation of Woodworth-Jefcoats et al. (2017) in the text to enhance context and support our
findings.
The largest concern I have is that the paper is predicated on a linkage between droughts and
historical declines in GoM catches that the authors do not demonstrate and which is not
supported by the cited peer-reviewed papers (nor by the large number of non-peer reviewed
technical reports that are cited). The authors postulate that a long (~3 year) drought in the mid- to
late 1980’s induced a decline in biomass and catch that is reflected in the timeseries for both.
These are plotted in Figure 1 (a) (e) and (f). However, one quickly notes that there are similar
large drops in the PDSI index in ~2000 and ~2012 but no similar subsequent drop in catch or
biomass timeseries as was seen in the late 1980’s. In the discussion section (lines 160-172) the
authors try to address this and explain it as a difference in drought length (3 yrs for the earlier
drought versus ~1 year for the others). This section is very speculative, without any
citations save for one at the end of the paragraph stating that the severity of the drought can be
related to the contrast between preceding wet years. In fact the largest concern I had in reading
this section was that there was no mention of possible changes in fishery management or markets
that could also explain the decline in catch.
We appreciate the reviewer's insightful comments regarding the linkage between droughts
and historical declines in Gulf of Mexico (GoM) catches. As noted in our manuscript, we
hypothesize that significant ecosystem impacts, reflected in declines in biomass and catches,
would primarily occur following prolonged severe droughts lasting three years or more.
This hypothesis is based on the understanding that short-lived species, such as Gulf
menhaden, can typically rebound through density-dependent compensatory processes after
brief periods of low productivity. However, extended periods of low productivity can
severely affect multiple year-classes, leading to long-term detrimental impacts on these
populations. We further clarify that the apparent effects of the 1980s drought can be partly
attributed to (1) elevated biomass and catches during the mid-1980s, following
exceptionally wet conditions in early 1982-1983, and (2) the high fishing effort prevalent
throughout the 1980s. (3) our extended time series (Supplementary section S2)
demonstrates that episodic fluctuations in menhaden populations correlate with highly dry
conditions (e.g., 2006, 2012) and wet periods (e.g., 2010).
To further address the reviewer’s concerns, we acknowledge that variations in fishery
management practices and market dynamics over time might also contribute to
fluctuations in catch. In the revised manuscript, we have included additional discussion on
these factors to provide a more comprehensive context for the observed changes in catch
and biomass.
Additionally, in response to the reviewer’s suggestion regarding the speculative nature of
the discussion, we have incorporated a new Supplementary section S6, which includes a
sensitivity analysis that evaluates the effects of prolonged versus shorter drought periods
(1- and 3- years duration). This analysis quantifies the potential impacts of different
drought durations and strengthens the robustness of our findings.
Additionally, following the sharp drop in in both catches and biomass in the late 1980’s catches
remain low while biomass increases, pointing towards a non-biomass driver of low catches (e.g.,
shift in management towards lower harvest mortality rates).
We appreciate the reviewer’s observations regarding the dynamics of catches and biomass
in the late 1980s. Indeed, from 1992 onwards, after the drought of the late 1980s, we
observed a gradual decline in catches, averaging approximately 3 t/km² over 24 years. This
trend aligns with the expected relationship described by the equation (C = F×B), where
fishing mortality (F) was reduced due to regulatory measures, consequently leading to
declining annual catches. This regulatory action facilitated an increase in the remaining
biomass within the marine ecosystem, fostering a more sustainable fish population.
To clarify this we added supplementary section S3, which illustrates the contrasting
relationship between menhaden catches and fishing effort in the 1980s (a non-intuitive,
drought-dominated relationship) and the shift towards a more intuitive relationship from
the 1990s onward.
Finally there are multiple disparate patterns in the magnitude and sometimes the direction of
biomass change and catch (this can be seen in Fig 1 (h) and (i); e.g., crab have the second largest
decline in biomass but increases in catch, similarly, younger menhaden had the larger declines in
biomass than older conspecifics but declines in older menhaden catches were larger than younger
ones). This is of course a not unexpected and well cited issue in fisheries, especially as biomass
declines where fishers can increase effort to offset declining biomass, or where catch declines
but is stabilized over time and biomass increases due to implementation of policies that reduce
harvest rates to sustainable levels. I believe the authors are aware of this issue (see plots of
relative effort) and offer what is maybe the most parsimonious explanation in the “model
limitation” section of the Methods (lines 506 -509):
506 “...For example, fluctuations in Gulf menhaden catches may be related to economic
processes, which occurred during the mid and late 1980s, when the Gulf menhaden fishery
underwent corporate consolidation resulting in declines in the number of fishing vessels and
processing plants. This may have contributed to the decline in catches 45. For species such as
Goliath grouper, declines in biomass and catch are likely a result of long periods of overfishing
or management regulations designed to reduce harvest (e.g., harvest moratorium).”
Similarly, the ESR (reference #1) states “The Gulf of Mexico Fisheries Management Council
implemented a number of Fishery Management Plans in the 1980s, and major Amendments
restricting fishing effort were passed in the 1990s.“ (p22).
We appreciate the reviewer’s valuable comment regarding the complex patterns observed
in biomass changes and catch dynamics. In addition, we indeed recognize that the
fluctuations in biomass and catch, such as the decline in crab biomass coinciding with an
increase in catch, are well-documented phenomena in fisheries science. To address these
complexities, we have enriched the "model limitation" section with further explanations
about the economic and regulatory factors at play, including the historical context of the
Gulf menhaden fishery and relevant management measures implemented over the years.
Additionally, we have included a non-fisheries-related index of juvenile Gulf menhaden
abundance in Louisiana estuaries. This data reveals a decline in the juvenile Gulf
menhaden population during the late 1980s that is unrelated to fisheries management
measures, further highlighting the influence of external environmental factors.
Of course these management measures could have been implemented to address the decline that
was driven initially by drought. The way to address how much climate drove the decline is to run
a hindcast or counterfactual simulation, although these are challenging with ecosystem models
because of model drift. So another approach would be to use a sensitivity simulation to evaluate
the hypothesis of prolonged drought versus short 1 year drought in driving declines. E.g., fixing
the F rate at a few different levels (e.g., those observed in the 1985-1990 period vs those
observed in 2013), simulate a) 3 year drought (sensu the 1985-1988) and b) a five year period
with a 1 year drought. Something like this should be conducted to demonstrate and support the
postulation that underlies the projection simulations. In the absence of the sensitivity simulation
above, there is not sufficient evidence provided presently to rule out changes in harvest pressure,
fisheries operations, management or markets in driving declines in catch in the late 1980’s
relative to early 1980’s. Given that the paper is predicated on the postulated relationship between
drought, nutrients, and declines in catches, establishing and supporting this is extremely
important. Additionally, I strongly suggest providing a historical time-series of harvest mortality
by age for menhaden (e.g., as a supplemental figure). It appears to my eye that the F rate for 1
year old fish is much higher during the 1985-1990 period than 2000 - 2016. Having the
timeseries would help facilitate comparisons in relative fishing pressure over time.
We thank the reviewer for the valuable insights. In response to the comments, we have

Additionally, we have incorporated the requested historical time series of harvest mortality
by age for Gulf menhaden, which can be found in Figure S2c. As noted by the reviewer,

the late 1980s can be attributed to higher fishing efforts and catches, while the later period

menhaden population.

menhaden fishing effort was actually declining during the 1980s, coinciding with a decline

We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comments regarding the second simulation. The
drought conditions for the specified years were computed based on the minimal moving
average of the 5th percentile PDSI value over a 5-year period, utilizing the variation from
the 20-member CMIP ensemble. This approach allows us to focus on the driest consistent
spells, which are of particular interest in our study. The correspondence between the driest
observed PDSI (indicated by magenta markers in Fig. 2a) and the modeled PDSI
(represented by the yellow shaded area) in Fig. 2a further justifies our emphasis on the 5th
percentile of the modeled PDSI.
While we acknowledge that wet periods corresponding to positive PDSI values will occur
within the projected time frames (through the end of the century), our focus on the impacts
of droughts necessitates prioritizing drought periods over wet ones. It is important to note
that the PDSI index is a "long-memory" index that accounts for soil moisture; thus, the
effects of very wet periods can diminish quickly following extreme hot and dry conditions.

scenario) from the mean and standard deviation of the ensemble for each time period in
order to provide error bars for the figures in Fig. 2c. We used the 5th percentile of the
modeled PDSI as the basis for our analysis based on the explanation above.

In addition, in response to the reviewer’s concern, we calculated the Modeling Efficiency
(MEF), a statistical metric that assesses how effectively our model predicts observed data
compared to using the mean of the observed values. While Ecosim models do not typically
yield a single measure of overall skill, modeling efficacy is often evaluated relative to the
model itself through Relative Model Efficiency (RME) and the Akaike Information
Criterion (AIC), as noted by Olsen et al. (2016).
Our analysis indicates that 74% of the fitted time series yielded positive MEF values,
suggesting that the model’s predictions are more accurate than those based on the mean of
the observed data for roughly three-quarters of the assessed time series. We have added
this information to the Methods section and included a supplementary section
