not explicitly model habitat–salinity interactions. Importantly, our ability to reproduce the
observed dynamics based solely on nutrient flow supports the principle of parsimony in
model design. We now note in the Methods (lines 825-828) as follows: “In addition, we did
not explicitly incorporate salinity–habitat interactions in our modeling framework. While
salinity increases during droughts can stress estuarine-dependent invertebrates (e.g., oysters,
shrimp)19, the ecosystem-wide declines observed here were reproduced based solely on nutrient
forcing, supporting a parsimonious focus on trophic mechanisms.”.
Lines 77-79: Once again, it should be made clear why this study focused on the impacts of river
flow on fisheries production in the GoM via trophic dynamics rather than habitat availability.
The previous paragraph states that the physical effects of river flow on invertebrates can be
important in the study area, but the next paragraph ignores this point.
We thank the reviewer for this helpful clarification request. In the revised text, we now
explicitly state that river flow can influence fisheries production in the Gulf of Mexico
through both physical (habitat–salinity) and trophic pathways. However, we clarify that
this study focuses on trophic dynamics for three reasons: (i) nutrient-driven productivity is
widely recognized as the dominant mechanism in this oligotrophic system, where oceanic
nutrient supplies are limited (e.g., Wissel and Fry, 2005), (ii) our ecosystem modeling
framework (EwE) is specifically designed to represent trophic interactions rather than
species-specific habitat–salinity responses, and (iii) the long-term datasets most consistently
available are those describing nutrient and productivity signals. We also acknowledge that
salinity-driven habitat effects represent an important complementary mechanism, and we
note this explicitly in the Introduction (lines 87–93) as follows: “In this study, we focus on
the trophic pathway for three main reasons. First, nutrient-driven productivity is widely
recognized as the dominant mechanism linking river flow to fisheries in this oligotrophic
system, where oceanic nutrient supplies from upwelling or currents are limited. Second, our
analytical framework is designed to represent trophic interactions at the ecosystem scale,
rather than species-specific habitat–salinity responses. Third, the available long-term data are
most consistent for nutrient inputs and productivity signals, making them more suitable for
quantitative analysis.”
Line 93: Please either define the abbreviation ‘MS’ or spell it out in full.
We thank the reviewer for noting this. In the revised manuscript, we have spelled out
“Mississippi (MS)” in full at first use to ensure clarity for all readers, followed by the
abbreviation in parentheses for subsequent mentions.
Line 105 (and elsewhere): All percentages should be presented to one decimal place to ensure
consistency throughout the paper.
We thank the reviewer for this comment. In the revised manuscript, we have reformatted
and rounded all percentage values to zero decimal places to ensure consistency throughout
the text.
Line 140: Add a comma after ‘(Fig. 2e,f)’.
We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. In the revised manuscript, we have added the
comma after “(Fig. 2e,f)” as recommended.
Line 144: This needs more explanation. Why would the effect of menhaden fishing mortality
decrease? If drought reduces the biomass of menhaden and its associated predators, then the
proportion of these stocks being exploited by fisheries would increase assuming status quo
fishing effort (i.e., the F value would increase at smaller stock sizes under constant fishing
effort).
We thank the reviewer for raising this point. In our Ecosim simulations, the reduced effect
of menhaden fishing mortality under drought arises from the foraging‐arena dynamics and
the strong bottom-up constraint imposed by nutrient limitation. Under severe drought
conditions, menhaden biomass remained low even at F=0, indicating that stock recovery
was prevented by food limitation rather than fishing pressure. At low stock sizes,
compensatory mechanisms (enhanced survival and growth) further reduce the sensitivity of
the stock to fishing, preventing complete collapse. This resilience to fishing mortality is
consistent with Gulf menhaden stock assessments and reflects their short-lived life history
and fishery selectivity patterns. Consequently, even under unchanged effort or F,
absolute
removals and the ecosystem-level footprint of fishing diminish relative to the dominant
bottom-up constraint imposed by drought. We have added a brief explanation of this
mechanism in the Results (lines 163-166) to clarify why the relative influence of F declines
when productivity and biomass are depressed as follows: “This reduced influence of fishing
mortality reflects the strong bottom-up limitation imposed by nutrient input, whereby
menhaden biomass remains low even when F is set to 0, and compensatory mechanisms
prevent collapse at low stock sizes. As a result, absolute removals and the ecosystem-level
footprint of fishing diminish relative to the dominant drought effect.”.
Line 161: Clarify what is being affected here. ‘The effect of variation in Gulf menhaden fishing
mortality on XYZ…’
We thank the reviewer for noting this ambiguity. In the revised manuscript, we now clarify
that this refers specifically to “the effect of variation in Gulf menhaden fishing mortality on
the biomass and catch of the GoM ecosystem, based on the examined functional groups.
Line 177: It is worth noting here that droughts can impact fishers’ harvesting behaviour.
Gillson (2011) describes that river flow can indirectly impact fisheries production by altering
the harvesting behaviour of commercial fishers.
We thank the reviewer for this observation. In the revised manuscript, we now note that
droughts can also influence fishers’ harvesting behavior. Freshwater flow can indirectly
affect fisheries production by altering the behavior of commercial fishers, who respond to
variable flows by opportunistically exploiting changes in species catchability. For example,
catchability of estuarine migrant species can increase during floods, while marine
estuarine-opportunist species may be more catchable during droughts. Recognizing this
behavioral component is important for understanding the full relationship between
freshwater flow and fisheries production, as it complements the ecological responses
considered in our analysis. We have incorporated this perspective into the text and cited
Gillson (2011) accordingly. The added text (lines 212-219) reads as follows: “Beyond
ecological processes, droughts can also influence fishers’ harvesting behavior, as variability in
freshwater flow alters species catchability and may drive commercial fishers to adjust their
targeting strategies17. Similar drought-induced shifts in species composition and fishing
practices have been documented elsewhere; for example, in eastern Australia, drought
conditions shifted landings from estuarine migrant species to marine estuarine-opportunist
species, accompanied by adaptive changes in effort and methods18. This behavioral
dimension, though not represented in our model, likely interacts with ecological responses and
adds an additional pathway by which drought affects fisheries production.”
Lines 212-213: It would be worth citing previous studies that have documented drought-induced
changes in species composition in marine ecosystems (e.g., Gillson et al., 2012).
We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. In the revised manuscript, we now cite Gillson
et al. (2012), which showed that drought can shift fisheries landings from estuarine migrant
species to marine estuarine-opportunist species. The added text in the Introduction (lines
60-68) reads as follows: “River flow has long been recognized as a “master variable”
regulating marine and estuarine ecosystems, influencing habitat availability, trophic
dynamics, and fishers’ harvesting behavior 15–19. Variability in river discharge controls
nutrient delivery, sediment transport, and salinity gradients, all of which shape the
productivity and distribution of marine organisms. In the GoM, a system otherwise strongly
oligotrophic with limited nutrient input from oceanic currents or upwelling, riverine nutrient
inputs are especially critical for sustaining fisheries yields 20. This highlights a trophic-driven
mechanism by which drought-induced reductions in river flow limit nutrient availability,
cascading through the food web to affect forage fish, predators, fish migration and
composition, and ultimately fisheries production.”.
Line 214: Amend this sentence as follows: ‘The declines in biomass and catches projected in our
study…’.
We have amended the sentence as requested.
Line 221: Are there also projections of how onshore and offshore wind might change in the
future? Wind conditions influence nutrient inputs by regulating upwelling and also affect the
distribution of pelagic fish larvae.
We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. Projections of future wind
conditions, both onshore and offshore, are available from regional climate modeling
studies, and these can indeed have important implications for the Gulf of Mexico
ecosystem, particularly in the west Florida shelf region, which is characterized by wind-
driven upwelling. While our study did not explicitly incorporate wind projections, we agree
that integrating this factor, especially under future climate scenarios, would provide a
more comprehensive understanding of potential changes in productivity and recruitment.
We note that this effect is expected to be more pronounced in major wind-driven upwelling
regions, such as the Eastern Boundary Upwelling Systems (e.g., California, Peru–Chile,
and Benguela/Namibia). We have added this point to the Discussion (lines 258-264) as
follows: “In addition to river flow, future changes in wind conditions could affect nutrient
delivery and recruitment in the GoM. Regional climate projections indicate shifts in onshore
and offshore winds, which regulate upwelling and larval dispersal, particularly along the west
Florida shelf. While not included in our simulations, incorporating wind forcing under
climate change scenarios would improve ecosystem projections. Such effects are expected to
be especially pronounced in major upwelling systems worldwide (e.g., California, Peru–Chile,
Benguela/Namibia)46.”.
Line 235: Replace ‘Gulf of Mexico’ with ‘GoM’, because this abbreviation has previously been
used earlier in the paper.
We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. We have replaced “Gulf of Mexico” with
“GoM” at line 235 to maintain consistency with the abbreviation used earlier in the
manuscript.
